MB. SINCLAIR-TRAVELLING EXPENSES OF MEMBERS BETWEEN RESIDENCE AND OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege affecting the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), myself, and every member in the house who comes from a distance to attend parliament. At the beginning of the last session we went to the accountant of the House of Commons and submitted our travelling expenses, along with receipts, in accordance with the Senate and House of Commons Act, section 43(1) of which states:
For each session of parliament, there shall also be allowed to each member of the Senate and of the House of Commons his actual moving or transportation expenses, and reasonable living expenses while on the journey between his place of residence and Ottawa, going and coming, once each way.
When we applied to the House of Commons accountant for payment of those expense accounts we were informed that Your Honour had ruled our accounts out of order. No reason was given, but the inference was that because we travelled by air our accounts were not in order.
I submit that the House of Commons Act makes no limitations as to the type of transportation to be used. When the first British Columbia members came here they came by sailing ship to San Francisco, across the continent by rail and then north by stage, for a matter of twenty-six days. Since that time we have had rail transportation; and since the advent of the Trans-Canada air lines, cabinet ministers, businessmen and civil servants have travelled back and forth by air. But we have been limited to travel by rail. If Your Honour will examine the public accounts for 1944 you will find that one Vancouver member travelled by air and at Easter adjournment in 1946 and 1947 members travelled by air. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) informs me that he regularly travels by air and his accounts are approved. For the pre-Christmas session, the British Columbia members who travelled by rail had to spend eight days
travelling to attend a session lasting eleven days. Moreover, those who went home by rail arrived only the day before Christmas.
We suffer enough by being absent from our homes for six months without having to drag ourselves across the continent by rail, and as a member of parliament I request that Your Honour give the reason which you gave to the accountant of the House of Commons as to why the expense accounts for the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and myself were refused.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PENSIONS AND STUDENT TRAINING ALLOWANCES -STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement to the house with respect to pensions and) student veterans' training allowances.
On the 19th December, 1947, I made a statement in this house respecting veterans pensions in the course of which I said that "in the case of disabled veterans and pensioned widows, the government will introduce legislation during the present session of parliament to amend the Pension Act, in order to provide for an increase in rates of compensation", and that such "increases will be made effective as of October 1, 1947".
During the recess of parliament the government continued to give careful consideration to the adequacy of the pensions in respect of disability and death, and particularly to the provision for dependents. Representations
Veterans Affairs

were received1 from the national organizations of ex-service men and women, and the entire situation was reviewed by the Department and by the government.
I am pleased to announce that a bill to amend the Pension Act is now virtually ready for introduction. I am prepared at once to give in outline what the government intends to propose:
(a)	The basic scale of pensions for total disability and death will be increased and, for all ranks up to and including that of captain, the compensation will be at a rate in excess of that at present being paid on behalf of captains.
(b)	The additional pension which is being paid on behalf of the wives and children of disability pensioners, and' the children of pensioned widows, will be substantially increased, as will the awards to orphan children.
(c)	The maximum award to the eligible parent or parents of a member of the forces who has died will be correspondingly increased.
With the consent of the house I shall now table a schedule reflecting the upward1 adjustments I have outlined. It is estimated that these adjustments over present rates will involve a total increase in cost of approximately $12,000,000.
These increased rates will, to a greater or lesser degree, affect over 400,000 persons and in accordance with my original announcement, will be effective from October 1. 1947. The government is anxious to have these retroactive payments made as early as possible. Although everything possible will be done to enable this to be accomplished, it will necessarily be a matter of some weeks, after authority is received, before the adjustment cheques can be ready.
The government has also been giving close and sympathetic consideration to the position of veterans in training, both vocational and university. It has been decided to change the schedule of training rates to provide increases to married veterans, and to those with dependents, in conformity with the rates in this schedule which I now table.
The effect of these increases will be as follows:	A married veteran while taking
training will receive $90 per month instead of $80. In addition, there will be payable on behalf of the first child $18 instead of $12, and for the second child $14, with proportionate increases for succeeding children, so that a married veteran with three children will receive $134 per month instead of $114. In addition to these rates, tuition fees will continue to be paid.

The increased rates are effective as from January 1, 1948. It is hoped that the increases will overcome many of the difficulties being experienced by married veteran students.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right, Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, on February 12, I indicated to the house that I would examine the press articles referred to by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Hamel) in his question of that day in connection with the new letters patent governing the office of Governor General of Canada. I have now had an opportunity of doing so and also of reading a subsequent article published in Le Devoir on February 13. This last article bears the title: "Mr. St. Laurent quite annoyed at the leakage of the state secret."
I hope I did not display any annoyance- which I certainly did not feel-though I was concerned to find that there had been any leakage about confidential correspondence between the Prime Minister of Canada and the secretary of His Majesty the King in his capacity as King of Canada. My concern was not over the contents of the correspondence but over the impropriety of publicity about something which, not only by tradition and by courtesy but also by proper constitutional practice, and even by the implication of the ministerial oaths of office, has always been and should be treated as highly confidential.
Of course it could be no secret that there must have been correspondence in connection 5849-79
with the new letters patent since it was apparent they were signed by His Majesty himself in London and authenticated under the Great Seal of Canada and countersigned by the Prime Minister of Canada in Ottawa. But the form and tenor of that correspondence was just as confidential as would have been their conversation if the Prime Minister of Canada had approached His Majesty in person at Buckingham Palace or elsewhere and the completion of the letters patent been arranged orally.
Nor -was it any secret that though the terms of these letters patent made it legally possible .for the governor general, on the advice of Canadian ministers, to exercise any of the powers and authorities of the crown iD respect of Canada, without the necessity of submission being made to His Majesty, including among others, royal full powers for the issuance of letters of credence for Canadian ambassadors and foreign ministers, there was no legal necessity to alter existing practices and that it would be the responsibility of the government of Canada, in any prerogative matter affecting Canada, to determine whether the submission should go to His Majesty or to the governor general.
What I have just stated was made perfectly clear to the press by the Prime Minister on October 1, 1947. What gave me some concern is the publication of garbled and speculative accounts of when this correspondence is supposed to have been exchanged and what it is supposed to contain.
Though the publication of the correspondence would at once dispel all this, the government is not disposed to take that easy way of dispelling it, because at best it would be discourteous to His Majesty and because of its possible effect as a precedent on confidential exchanges of views between the sovereign and his responsible advisers in relation to public affairs prior to decisions or actions for which his advisers themselves and they only have full constitutional responsibility.
Le Devoir in its article of February 13 narrows its alleged disclosures to one assertion. After discussing the Prime Minister's communication to the press it says in so many words:
The only newr fact asserted by Le Devoir is the existence of a personal communication of the king expressing the desire that our ambassadors' letters of credence continue to be submitted to him for signature. It is precisely this royal communication which constitutes the state secret w'hich it was desired to keep inviolate.
Diplomatic Service

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
After making that assertion, the paper states:
The Canadian people have the right to know if King George VI did express, in a communication to the Canadian government, a personal desire which would amount to_ an intrusion of the government of Great Britain in our foreign politics. The Canadian people also have the right to know if the king expressed this desire before the issuance of the new letters patent or only during the last weeks.
I feel I can say this much: There has been no communication whatsoever from His Majesty referring to the manner in which it would be agreeable to him to have letters of credence to Canadian ambassadors and ministers dealt with since May, 1947 and there has been no communication at any time which would amount to an intrusion by the government of Great Britain in our foreign politics.
Any suggestion that His Majesty may have been acting on advice of the United Kingdom ministers in the course of the correspondence with the Prime Minister of Canada about these letters patent 'is fantastic. I will merely recall, because it is too clear to require any comment, that the right to advise His Majesty in prerogative matters affecting Canada resides exclusively in the government of Canada.
The conference on the operation of dominion legislation held in London in 1929 to provide for the implementation of the declaration of the imperial conference of 1926, made the following declaration:
It is the right of the government of each dominion to advise the Crown in relation to all matters relating to its own affairs.
The report of this conference was approved by the imperial conference of 1930.
This was followed by the statute of Westminster, 1931, which refers to the declarations and resolutions set forth in the reports of these conferences and makes the legislative provisions required to ratify, confirm and establish such of these declarations and resolutions as it was necessary to deal with by legislation.
The new letters patent in increasing the powers of the governor general represent a very significant constitutional advance in line with the declarations of the conferences and the statute of Westminster. To suggest that there has been anything whatsoever which could be regarded as retrogressive in connection therewith or in connection with the practices thereunder is absolutely unwarranted.
What I have already said disposes also of the assertion in the article of the Chicago Tribune referred to by the hon. member. With regard to the references in that article to the appointment of Mr. Edmond Turcotte, I

need only say this: The correspondence relating to the new letters patent and to what was intended to be the practice thereunder took place several months before Mr. Tureotte's appointment. Moreover, Mr. Turcotte was not appointed ambassador or minister. He was appointed consul general, an appointment of a different character, which was made by order of His Excellency the Governor General in council on the 27th of October last.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS IN HALIFAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Labour of which I have given him notice? The radio this morning announced that there were 7,500 unemployed in the city of Halifax, with a possible layoff of 2,000 more within the month. Has the minister been advised of this? Is his department taking any steps with regard to employment or relief measures in that city, and has he checked with the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), who might have a solution?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS IN HALIFAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the employment situation in certain sections of the maritimes, including Cape Breton, New Glasgow and Halifax, has been receiving special attention for several weeks past. The situation at Halifax has considerably worsened in the last few days on account of the sudden drop in shipping.
The rather unfavourable situation in the maritimes is explained by a number of circumstances. The freight traffic through the maritime ports has reached an all-time low since before the war.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS IN HALIFAX
speechtext: That is government policy for you.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS IN HALIFAX
speechtext:
I shall not say what I might have said. The cut of 'logs for lumber has been lighter this year and lumbermen have not been in as great demand as heretofore. Shortages of material, especially steel, have affected work in the shipyards and layoffs have occurred. Other industries have also had to curtail on account of the shortage of material. On Saturday the Halifax shipyards laid off 300 men. For the first time since the war the textile plants report sufficient staff and there are no vacancies other than for skilled workers.
With regard to the immediate situation in Halifax city and county I was advised at noon today that there were registered in our Halifax office a total of 4,187 men and
Inquiries of the Ministry

women seeking employment. That is a drop of 3,000 from my hon. friend's figure.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS IN HALIFAX
speechtext: My figure came over the radio this morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS IN HALIFAX
speechtext:
You cannot believe
everything you hear, even over the radio. Unemployment insurance benefits were being paid to 2,728 of the persons registered for employment. This, of course, does not mean that some of the others who are not being paid are not eligible for benefits. They may have been laid off in the last few days. It simply means that in many cases they have not been out of work long enough to claim the benefits. In addition, there are 1,800 stevedores on the stevedores' register, and there were fewer than 400 working today. The department has been giving close attention to the situation particularly that which has existed in Cape Breton and New Glasgow. Men out of work, and some women too, have been offered free transportation to other parts of Canada. This offer has, in fact, been standing for several months. Up to date 2,632 persons have been moved by the department.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS IN HALIFAX
speechtext: Never send another notice or you will get more of this.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS IN HALIFAX
speechtext:
I shall tell the whole story, and leave nothing to the imagination.
While I am on the subject I should like to state that a good deal of construction is being planned in the maritimes. Halifax city has under consideration a housing project, of 300 units. A new pier and emigration shed at east Saint John is at the planning stage. East Saint John has a plan underway for a housing project.
Contracts have been let to the Saint John Dry dock company for a wharf construction job to cost $2,500,000. The provincial governments are planning for a heavy program of highway and bridge construction for the coming season. Two of the brickyards have closed down and are remodelling so that they can increase their production. The Nova Scotia power commission has announced a $5,000,000 program of hydro development. All of these things lead one to believe that the present situation is largely seasonal in character.
There are some very encouraging things that should be reported; for example, close to one million crates of New Brunswick seed potatoes have been shipped from the port of Saint John to Argentina and other South American countries during the past three months, the arrangements for which shipments were due to the activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

There has been a very brisk movement of maritime woodsmen to the United States for lumber work, and many Canadian workers have taken advantage of the offer of employment in the United States and will be returning with a considerable number of United States dollars.

speechtext:
I do not want to delay the committee for more than a minute or two, Mr. Chairman, but I thought. I should say a word before the minister speaks. I have been giving some consideration to the amendment now before the committee. After weighing both sides of the question.-and I admit that there are definitely two sides to it- I must say that I find myself more in favour of the amendment than I was when it wras proposed the other night. As I say, I realize that there are two sides to the question and I have given consideration to the side which the minister has indicated in a number of his speeches with regard to the things that might make him fearful about having such an amendment passed. I think the minister indicated last week that action of the house in passing an amendment of this kind would possibly be looked upon by the United States as a breach of faith on Canada's part. They may do so, Mr. Chairman, but certainly not reasonably. The Geneva pact recognizes that where a nation finds itself with an adverse balance of trade, such as Canada now does, that nation may have to use the escape clause that is .provided .in the pact and restrict imports from all their creditor nations. Surely no fair-minded person or nation would regard as a breach of faith the action we are now proposing to take. If the authorities in the United States hold to the principle of nondiscrimination and are favourable to the insertion of an escape clause for nations that have an unfavourable balance of trade, surely they expect us to use it if we get into that position. Likewise, I think the United States would not consider the amendment that is before the committee as a breach of faith, if we should carry it, particularly in the light of the fact that that great nation has never yet been seized with a sense of her own responsibility to balance her trade in the interests of world peace. I cannot believe that the United States would resort to retaliation, as has been suggested, if we took action to protect our dollar reserves and our trading position while at the same time we take *perfectly legal action such as is envisioned in this amendment to protect our own people, and do it under the terms of the Geneva pact. No one can argue that it is not protection of our own people to swing some of the trade that is being lost, through restricting United States imports, to sterling countries from which we can get a certain quantity of the things which cannot come into Canada now under these restrictions.
At one stage in this debate the minister stated that the amount of business we could swing to sterling countries as a result of th<
Foreign Exchange Conservation

restriction on United States imports would be comparatively small. If that is so-and the minister nods his head-then it is one more good reason why it would not be looked upon as a breach of faith if we were to accept this amendment. In the light of the suggestion that the amount of business might be comparatively small, I do not see why the United States would be expected to retaliate against Canada by restricting exports from that country to Canada, including essentials, such as oil, steel, cotton and other products.
I am sure if the minister would assure the United States that the restrictions against her goods would be removed as quickly as Canada can get herself in a safe position, so far as trade is concerned, into a position where our dollar reserves were not in jeopardy, and would come clean with them, the United States would understand and certainly would not consider that, in passing this amendment, we are committing a breach of faith.
One further point before taking my seat, and it is this; we are going to have negotiations in future with the United States government. I believe it was a good thing to have the amendment offered in committee last week if for no other reason than to bring home to the people of the United States the fact that we take a serious view of this w'hole business. I should like to have it impressed upon those good folk down there, for whom I have the greatest respect, the obligation they take upon themselves when they assume leadership in the world trade. Something has to be done to bring home to the American people that they have an obligation to do things to balance their own trade, and thus to help lesser nations industrially, to balance theirs, so as to take care of their own people.
Whether or not the amendment is accepted, I contend that the salutary effect will be good, and particularly if a substantial portion of this House of Commons votes for it-as I propose to do. I believe such action would strengthen the hands of the minister in his future negotiations with that great nation to the south of us; and for that reason, along with many others, I propose to support the amendment.

speechtext:
Coming from Ontario I should like to call attention to the importance of Bill No. 3, to which an amendment has been offered by the hon. member for Kinders-ley. He has moved-
That subsection 1 of section 3 of Bill No. 3 be amended by inserting after the word "Canada" in line nine on page one of the said bill the following words:
"from any country requiring gold or currency of the United States of America in payment or settlement of their purchase price."

The subsection would then read:
No person shall import or attempt to import into Canada from any country requiring gold or currency of the United States of America in payment or settlement of their purchase price any goods listed or of the classes described in schedules I, II or III.
If the section in the bill is followed it is good-bye to any trade with soft currency countries, including Great Britain, France.
Italy, Holland, Belgium, Luxembourg and the rest of them.
I should like to make one or two comments about this bill, because thus far I have not taken part in the debate. I did not read the bill until a few days ago. In my view this bill takes us back to where we were years ago. When I asked about the Geneva charter on February 7, I was told nothing whatever about it. This whole thing came in November last like a bolt from the blue. Those people who sat at Geneva were free traders-and they assembled in a good place. What they have done in these pacts has caused disaster to both small and large business in Canada.
We are back to where we were in the days of Gladstone, when Great Britain was a free trading country, and when Liberals in this house were free traders. We find that the first schedule of the bill is the prohibitory schedule, while schedule II gives the quotas and schedule III the permits. Anyone who will look at Bill No 3 will see that it is based on the Geneva charter; and if we look into the definition of "charter" we find that the bill includes something which was never intended by the writers of the Oxford dictionary. According to the Oxford dictionary a charter was a grant from the sovereign or from a legislature. That definition was stretched at the time of the Atlantic charter to embrace the visionary hopes of the late President Roosevelt on behalf of the United States.
If we look at this bill, what do we find? I asked about it last February. A meeting was held at Geneva while parliament was in session here at Ottawa, but on February 7, the government said it did not know anything about it. The government has not yet been able to sell this program to the country, because both large and small businesses are affected. Some of them have been practically ruined by it. They want to import commodities such as fresh vegetables from the West Indies, but they are not permitted to do so. They say America would claim this is discriminatory. Mr. Churchill spoke about the matter yesterday, and his statement is reported by the press in this way:
Turning to home affairs, Churchill attacked socialist planners who he said "keep the British

Foreign Exchange Conservation
bulldog running around after his own tail till he is dizzy and then wonder that he cannot seep the wolf from the door."
That is what we are trying to do in Canada. We are trying to keep the wolf from the doors of large and small manufacturers. But we are lucky in this country to be permitted to breathe the fresh air without first having to get a permit under this bill.
I believe this has been overdone; the government of the day and the Liberal party for two generations on trade policies has done everything by fits and starts and nothing long. In the matter of trade, I can remember when the Canadian council of agriculture came here to Ottawa, in 1923, the first year the Drury government took office, and they said protection was an unmitigated evil and they would get a spade and dig up the last remnant of it in Canada. They claimed that the grain growing industry was not an east and west industry, but a north and south industry, to serve the United States rather than England, France, Italy, and the allied countries who were with us in the first war.
I can tell you this, that the government of the day has no mandate for this bill. Where do they get their mandate for everything that has been done to upset the whole fiscal and economic system of this country set up in Canada since confederation? Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding were two of the founders of the preferential system, and it is top bad that that was dropped by the United States-Canada treaty in 1938. I was one who along with the Social Crediters opposed the Bretton Woods agreement and showed the folly of the American loan, because I saw then the disaster coming from Geneva last summer. I saw it coming back in 1945. I knew what was going to happen. In my address with respect to the Bretton Woods agreement I predicted that we would have the very state of affairs that has developed, and we could go back to the days of unrestricted reciprocity with the United States covering every article of trade and commerce and upsetting our whole fiscal system. Considering the natural resources and the raw materials of Britain it is strange to me that the mother country and the dominions did not stay together, in peace as in war. Unless they hang together in trade and commerce and defence and migration they are going to hang seperately, because no dominion can go it alone. We will find this out during the coming summer and fall if this bill passes.
This Bill No. 3 is no protection by any means whatever. What has happened since we came into this house? Before and during the last war there were nin* or ten different 5849-80
forms of protection applied to the farming industry of this country. I admit that some were necessary. There were those in this house who said that protection was an unmitigated evil, yet during the war we gave the. farmers seven or eight kinds of protection. In fact for years Canada paid them a bonus not to grow crops at all.
When I saw the war coming I spoke in the house and suggested to the Minister of Agriculture and the government and asked that storage reservoirs be built in the old country in which to store our grain. In January 1938 the British Medical Association said that hard grains and wheat could be stored scientifically below ground and kept for ten years. But they would not do that at all. They paid people not to grow crops; they had acreage bonuses and all that kind of thing, all by protectionist measures.
I take exception to this third section of the bill because it is not protection in any sense of the word. It ruins any chance of protection for the small storekeeper, the small importer of goods, the industrial worker and the farmer. It contains many discriminatory clauses. This Bill No. 3, section 3 and the three schedules, ruin any hope of the people in the soft currency countries of doing any export business with this country.
These are all discriminatory agreements. They go beyond our national policy. What is our national policy? Sir John A. Macdonald in 1878 laid it down and Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding adopted it. They were the authors of preferential trade which was abrogated to the United States in 1938. Because of that we had soup kitchens all over the country. Our policy was to have our own markets for our own products and our own work for our own workmen. The United States pulled themselves up from the dark days when the commercial travellers from Great Britain went through their land selling goods. They are today the greatest industrial country in the world and they achieved that greatness by having the highest protection of any country. Now they want to .extend the Hyde Park agreement which is not an agreement at all, which is simply a verbal agreement. I am opposed to the trade pacts made in Geneva. I am against the whole idea of multilateral trade agreements and the manner of putting through this bill.
No conference was held last January before the February Geneva meeting. New Zealand asked for a conference and so did the mother country and Australia, but what did Canada tell them? We had the reply, when I raised it in the house, that the government did not
Foreign Exchange Conservation

intend to hold such a meeting. They sent Mr. Wilgress over there and he is down in Havana now at a trade conference of twenty-one countries. According to a dispatch published in the press last week he said in Havana that 800 amendments have been proposed to the Geneva charter, not one of which can be accepted because it is all signed, sealed and delivered by twenty-one countries; not a line of it can be changed.
By this Bill 3, clause 3, the various subsections of clause 3 and three schedules we are only holding a post mortem. We are just caretakers and undertakers. That is what we should turn ourselves into, because that is all the .power we have over this particular bill. It has been signed, sealed and delivered by the twenty-one governments and by the permanent officials. The government of the day will have to take the responsibility.
As I say, there was no conference before Geneva. New Zealand, Australia and Great Britain wanted a conference. The United States should have been told that preferential trade was a family matter and would not be open for discussion at Geneva. If that had been done w-e would not have had the situation we have today.
By the Geneva pact the Liberal party has gone back on everything Sir Wilfrid Laurier did. What did he say in 1897 when he was first in the diamond jubilee procession over there? He said, "If you want our aid, invite us to your councils." We were invited in February, 1947, to the councils of Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand, as to Geneva, but we would not even attend them before Geneva. We are simply hanging all hope of preferential trade in the future on the sour apple tree with John Brown's body. The action of the Liberal party puts me in mind of the old song, "Rocked in the cradle of the deep, I lay me down in peace to sleep." That is what happened at Bretton Woods and Geneva; they were rocked in the cradle of the deep and they laid themselves down in peace to sleep. They did the same thing at Geneva.
I am not here to criticize the United States; it is a great land and what they did in the war was wonderful; but I think they would appreciate us more if we told them the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth about where these bargains are going to land this country.
Canadianism defeated eontinentalism at the polls in 1911. Canada's victory on the reciprocity issue should have cleared the way for the working out of a protectionist system that would protect the consumer against unjust

prices just as truly as that system would protect the manufacturer against unjust competition. Canadianism has been perverted more and more into a system of taking care of the producer and leaving the consumer to take care of himself. The desire of the milling companies and the middlemen to inflate the price of their securities on the market is much more conspicuous than the desire of these milling companies to pay the farmer a fair price for wheat or to charge the consumer a fair price for flour. Greed on the part of manufacturers and Ottarva's failure to restrain their greed has weakened the whole principle of Canadianism in this country's trade and industry.
Someone mentioned the flag the other night in connection with this party. In 1922 I said that it would be better for the Conservative party to remain out of power under the union jack of Canadianism than to be returned to power under the white flag of unrestricted reciprocity or the yellow flag of free trade.
This Bill No. 3 is going back to the days of Gladstone and the old free trade way of doing business when we started up as a country. It is brought in under the guise of an emergency but it is going to be here for a long time. We are giving up all hope of ever restoring the preferential system of trade with the British empire. I am opposed to this internationalism and multilateral trade. I have opposed it before because it has brought this country only a minimum of trade as compared with preferences. True, we had a policy once of favoured-nation trade with twenty-eight countries, and that was a good system, although it encouraged trade with some countries only, not with the vast majority. National combinations can be more easily controlled from Ottawa than international combinations or cartels can be restrained or suppressed from Washington.
Away back in 1923, I brought up the question of a Canadian national coal policy which would have saved us millions of United States dollars. I brought it up almost every session. I also brought up the question of developing oil from the tar sands, and the question of asbestos. All our coal should be mined under the British flag, from Wales, the maritimes and Alberta. In 1913, 1914 and 1915 we had ships coming into Toronto harbour loaded with coal from Swansea, Wales. They had come all the way across the ocean and up the St. Lawrence and docked in Ashbridge's bay, owned by Baldwin's, with which the late Stanley Baldwin was connected. That just shows what can be done. Ten years later

______ Foreign Exchange Conservation
millions of tons of coal were brought in under that policy from the same three places, and we could have ten times as much if only we solved the transportation problem by water and rail and all rail.
I came across an article today proposing to stop the flow of our minerals in their raw state to the United States, to be manufactured there into finished products. The Hon. T. A. Crerar in an address to the Canadian Club at Hamilton said that Canada was overindustrialized. I pointed out that Canada's yearly imports of products from the United States which under a proper policy could be bought in Canada amounted to $400 million, and showed that $9,000,000 w'orth of raw asbestos exported from the province of Quebec is shaped and fashioned by United States hands into a finished product worth $60,000,000. Think what it would mean if that work were done in our own country. I also pointed out that in processing this asbestos, 15.000 United States citizens were employed, receiving wages of $25,000,000 per annum and supporting a population across the line of 75,000. My address was commented upon in an editorial written by John R. Robinson, a great editor, in the Toronto Evening Telegram of May 14, 1924. I also pointed out that the number of workers in the United States employed in the manufacture of exports of raw materials from Canada was 120,000, and that the United States population supported by the sale of these exports was at least 700.000. Think of what such a policy would mean today when we are short of United States dollars. I believe the time has come when we should raise this issue. We are going to have trouble in respect to trade with the Argentine. Agreements have been made for the purchase by Britain of Argentine cattle and food and grains. We should have stayed with preferences to the mother country and the sterling area and then we should not have had all this trouble. Although things may look dark in Great Britain, she is not going to be crippled for ever, and we should do everything we can to build up our trade with her.
I am going to vote against the Geneva agreements. I do not believe in them. They upset the whole economic policy of this country since confederation and will cause wide unemployment. They are not in the interests of Canada, not in the interests of our farmers, or industrial workers, not in the interests of the mother country, and not in the interests of the empire. We should stick to the British preferential system which did so much for us after the dark days after the first world war. This Geneva business means the ruination of this country and will lead to 5849-80^
widespread unemployment here. The government of the day should have an election on this issue. They have no mandate from the people of this country to overthrow our whole traditional policy. This country is heading for disaster the moment we throw overboard the trade policy we have followed since confederation.

Mr. Chairman, I assure you my remarks will be brief; but after listening to the debate I did1 feel that I should express the views of one from the maritime provinces. During the debate we have heard a great deal about trade between the United States and Canada. I am sure that if some hon. members who have tala n part fn the debate had lived and were livit g in the maritime provinces they would take a different attitude.
It is all right to talk about trade in the sterling areas when you have articles that can be traded' in those areas; but when you have a perishable article it is difficult to trade in other countries. Figures were put on the record today by the Minister of Labour showing that last year in Charlotte county the sardine catch amounted to almost two million cases. These were caught in the southern part of Charlotte county.. Nearly a million and1 a half cases were sold in the United States. Those that were canned in Canada were to a great extent exported; but I want to point out to the committee that down where I come from the people will resent any measure or regulation- that interferes with trade between the United States and Canada.
During the discussion I have also heard remarks such as the one we heard away back in 1911, "no truck or trade with the Yankees". When you give expression to those views in the maritime provinces you find a people there who take a very different view, and I believe the same applies all over Canada. Another thing that strikes me is that on many occasions in this country we forget too quickly. In listening to the discussion I often wondered if we ever thought back to the last war. I am thinking particularly of the canning industry. I realize that I talk mostly about fish, but I am once more thinking of the canning industry. During the war, from 1940 to 1945, if it had not been for the help of our southern neighbours, the canning industry in Charlotte county, and in fact in the whole of the maritime provinces, would have been closed. We depended one hundred per cent on our United States friends for tin plate. I am sure hon. members realize that during the war tin plate was in very short supply. We had none at all in Canada. In the canning industry
Foreign Exchange Conservation

we did! mot lose a single day on account of a shortage of 'tin plate, thanks to our United States friends to the south.
Edible oils are used extensively in the sardine industry; in fact it is utterly impossible to carry on the industry without them. There again we depended one hundred per cent on our United States friends. Prior to the war we imported! cotton seed oil from Great Britain. During the war the only thing available in the way of edible oil for canning purposes was soy beam oil from tihe United States. Not one single day was lost in Charlotte county on account of a shortage of edible oil.
When we are speaking of our neighbours to the south there is one other thing we should keep in mind. During the period of the war they were supplying us with gasoline. The rations that the people of this country were given, compared favourably with and in some cases were better than those given to their own citizens in the United States.
When mention is made of interference or a suggestion of interference with the trade over that border I say that it would not meet with the approval of the people of the maritime provinces. I for one am firmly convinced that the freer goods move over that border both ways the greater the prosperity in the maritime provinces, and I shall oppose any measure, any regulation which in any -way interferes with the traffic we have enjoyed' for years and years.
In closing I would ask horn, members to give this matter very serious thought. As I have explained to hon. gentlemen, down where I live we have a perishable article to dispose of. It must go to the United States market. The United States fishermen in Maine have for years and years tried' to convince the powers that be in Washington that Canadian fish and fish products should not go into the United States in competition with their own. Regardless of the arguments put-forward1 by these fishermen we still enjoy that market, and without it today the fishing industry, not only in my own county of Charlotte but in the maritime provinces as a whole, would be practically worthless.
Our lobster industry last year was fairly prosperous. I should like once more to put the figures on record. One company alone in a little town where I live exported $4,000,000 worth of lobsters to the United States market in 1945. Bess than four per cent of that amount were sold in Canada. That will give the committee some idea of what the United States markets mean to ihe fishermen in the maritime provinces. I would therefore ask

hon. members to think carefully before supporting this measure, because the people down in my part of the country will very much resent any regulation which will in any way interfere with that international trade.

The best way to answer the question is this: We cannot get the currency of the United States through the form which our trade has taken in past years. IVith the exception of a few years during the war the United States have sold on this market more goods than we have been able to supply them in return; and it is to correct that deficiency, I presume, that the Minister of Finance has introduced1 this measure and the others which are to follow.
The hon. member for Charlotte of course is quite correct in his argument, and I agree with him, except that he does not carry it to its logical conclusion. Undoubtedly we want to sell to the United States as much as they sell to us. Apparently that is the only way in which international trade can be carried on at the present time, because the British link on which we relied before the war is broken for the time being. That, of

________________Foreign Exchange Conservation
course, is the crux of the whole situation, and I think the government would be first to admit that it is true.
In this bill the Minister of Finance has presented three schedules. Schedule I includes lists of goods which are under complete import Dan; schedule II includes goods which are permitted to be imported on a quota basis related1 to the pre-war imports from the countries of origin; schedule III allows all imports by permit only.
The argument of the Minister of Finance in turning down this amendment-because I presume that is what the government proposes to do, or it would have accepted the amendment long ago-is that the goods involved in the three schedules, goods which are under import restriction from the United States and from the soft currency countries, will give us imported articles from the soft currency countries in excess of what we would get from the United States.
The minister gave us certain figures when he introduced the bill, but the unfortunate thing is that these figures are not complete. I would ask the minister, before he turns down this amendment, to give us an assurance that before the bill is finally concluded, before we have considered the individual items in the three schedules, he will prepare a concrete table enumerating the items in the three schedules and indicating wtiat will be the dollar effect of his ban in the form it is taking in relation to United States imports and from the point of view of future imports from other countries. He has indicated that the various items, for example, in schedule II which are subject to quota based on the 1939 import experience will be less unfavourable to the soft currency countries than would appear on the surface. I think it is only fair that the minister should give us a detailed table before the bill is concluded. That is what I would ask at the present time.

speechtext: When the minister is preparing that table will it be possible, in the matter of schedule I and the quotas of schedule II, to set opposite those items which ones can be imported from the soft currency countries, which we could have if they were not banned or under quota?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I will see what accurate data I can give on that. In my speech introducing the bill, particularly at pages 333 and 334 of
Hansard, there is a good deal of information on that subject, and I will see what additional information I can give.
A good many hon. gentlemen have expressed concern that the exchange conservation measures which the government has introduced, and in particular this bill, will have an adverse effect on British exports to Canada, and on several occasions I have expressed the belief that the reverse will be the case.
In the first place, I direct the attention of the committee to the statistics which have now become available for December, 1947, that is, the first full month during which the program was in effect. In December, 1947, the total Canadian imports from the United Kingdom were valued at $20,254,000, as compared with $11,664,000 the preceding December. The increase was about 73 per cent. I might add that the December, 1947, figure is higher than that for any previous month in the year and, I am informed, in no other postwar month have commercial imports, exclusive of Canadian war materials returned from the United Kingdom, been so large.
I do not believe the fears that this conservation program will injure our trade with Britain are well founded. It is evident. I think, that they are not based on experience to date, and I am confident that future figures will emphatically dispel that fear.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Is it not an obvious fact that if these restrictions and quotas were not in effect, imports from Great Britain and the other non-dollar countries would have been even larger than the figures the minister has given?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: No. They would have been smaller, because prohibitions and quotas against the dollar areas are so strong that they enabled British goods to come in during that month and will continue to allow British goods to come in, which otherwise would have competition from United States products, textiles in particular. The competition would have been such that it would have excluded British products.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I said that if the prohibition against goods from Britain had not been in effect there would 'have been more imports from Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I cannot agree with my hon. friend for the reason I have given, that the effect of the quota system was such as to enable Britain to export to us in the month of December, and she is continuing to export to us, goods she would not have been able to send on a competitive basis with the United States; and the comparatively minor prohibitions
Foreign Exchange Conservation

have been very much more than offset by these added imports. That is assertion, I know, but it is based on information. Let me finish this statement and I will answer any further questions later.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The minister missed the point entirely. The point was that if the prohibitions had been in effect against the United States and other dollar countries but not against Britain and other soft currency countries, then the imports from those countries would have been greater, of necessity, than the figures the minister gave.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
That is true, no doubt, if the quotas had been on a different basis. But one must take the program as a whole. You cannot take schedule I and ignore schedules II and III. The point is that the net effect of schedules I and II is to stimulate trade from the United Kingdom and the soft currency country areas as against the dollar area. Nearly all consumer products which Britain is in a position to send in volume are listed in schedule II and accordingly, as I said before, British exporters are afforded an opportunity and a strong incentive to step in and fill the gap which results from quota restrictions on competitive imports from dollar countries. The quotas under schedule II are non-discriminatory in form. But of course they take prewar imports as the base, and by assisting Britain to regain her pre-war share of the import market they are in fact of tremendous benefit to her. The complete prohibitions of schedule I did affect British trade but only to a slight extent. As I said on January 30, the prohibited list then covered only about two and a quarter millions of United Kingdom imports, and even this figure has since been reduced to some extent by the amendments which I have subsequently announced. The amount is less than 1J per cent of the total imports from that country to Canada.
Hon. members will note that in respect of textile products, which is the most important quota category, imports from schedule countries, namely, the hard currency countries, are being cut down, from $130,000,000 to $40,000,000. On the other hand, the nonschedule countries, primarily the United Kingdom, are given an incentive to increase their exports to this country from $52,000,000 to $120,000,000. Similar opportunities on a smaller scale are afforded other British goods by quotas applicable to such things as prepared food, leather products and miscellaneous products including glassware, cutlery, sporting goods and toys. I can only repeat that I am convinced that the effect of this

bill will be to help Britain to trade with Canada instead of injuring her under existing circumstances.
Amendment negatived: yeas, 42; nays, 49.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
On section 3 of this bill I want to follow up something I took up early in the session in connection with the importation of fruits and vegetables. While the hon. member for Charlotte was speaking I was thinking that, while he talked about the freer trade with the United States as the Liberal policy, never in the history of this country have tariffs been so high as they are at the present moment, and more are proposed. It is a case of talking in one way and acting in another. The Minister of Agriculture has now admitted that the agricultural policy during the war years and since, when our farmers were denied the United States market for their products, was not a marketing policy on the part of the government but a price control policy, and the farmers were the victims of it. In some of these schedules that are being introduced the farmers are again becoming the victims of that policy. It is not a policy of developing the natural resources of this country. We have thousands and thousands of idle acres that could be growing the food which we import from the United States, but who dares to go into that business, because nobody knows when this particular dollar conservation program may end and unrestricted importation of food from the United States will ruin those men who have gone into that business.
We have an immigration policy, if it can be called one, under which we are bringing in people from Europe, many of whom are skilled in the production of fruits and vegetables. I am thinking particularly of those who come from Holland. They could very well turn their skill to the production of many of the things we have been importing from the United States. We could establish them on land. But what is the use? In a matter of months, the minister said, the policy will be over. We should arrive at something definite. We cannot be going in two directions at once. We should have a policy under which our farmers can go ahead, plan their future, and know whether they can expand their operations or not.
While this committee in investigating prices I suppose mention of that matter should not be made, but I just wish to refer back to the thirties. A great deal has been heard here about cheap food. Back in the thirties we had cheap food; eggs were eight cents a dozen; wheat was thirty-five to sixty cents a bushel;

Foreign Exchange Conservation
milk for cheese purposes ran from fifty-six to sixty cents. What happened? Thousands of people were walking the streets looking for jobs. Why? Because farmers could not purchase the things which are manufactured in our cities. So let us not enter into some plan that will bring about cheap food. The day we have cheap food we shall have idle men.
I would say that this policy is a two-faced one. It is designed to discourage United States trade, so the minister says; and then he says it is designed for freer trade. I wonder what will happen. One minister says it is a long-term program and the next minister says it is a short-term plan. What are we to believe? The minister has said that he will not protect Canadian producers. He also said that the 25 per cent excise tax is designed to protect United States manufacturers who were exporting to this country. I wonder just whom the cabinet represents. Does it represent United States producers of the goods which we have been importing, or does it represent United States farmers who have been sending in thousands of carloads of farm produce to an agricultural country. If I had known different, I would have thought I was listening to Clinton Anderson, the Secretary of Agriculture in the United States or Averell Harriman, Secretary of Commerce in the United States, instead of our own cabinet minister.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: You likely were.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Canadian growers are not asking for something impossible. They are just asking'for an opportunity to grow and to market the things they can produce in this country. Let me give an illustration of what is going on. Here in my hand I have two letters sent out by organizations which are dealing with fruits and vegetables. One is issued by the Ontario food council and is signed by M. M. Robinson as manager. This is special newsletter 5B, dated May 23, 1947, and is dealing with the importation of lettuce. It was designed to advise growers and importers with regard to the situation as far as that one particular product was concerned. It says:
Lettuce available June 2.
We are now informed, after a careful cheek, that head lettuce will be ready for harvest in the Leamington area June 2 with some supplies available the end of next week.
Favourable growing conditions during the last few days have brought some early vegetables on with a rush. Conditions during the past week for growth could not have been better -and the original expectation that lettuce would not be available until June 9 has had to be revised.
There is a lot of head lettuce in the Leamington area and generally it is of excellent quality so far. Actually, the weather could not be better for lettuce and cabbage.
Please co-operate by calling off imported lettuce deal as quickly as possible.
Actually what happened after this information. had gone out was that importers brought in as large a quantity as it was possible to buy of head lettuce and stored it, and practically ruined the Canadian growers who had passed out this information that it would be available so that they could have protection for the time it was necessary to have it. That is one of the results of "kindly cooperate". The government did not. The grower did.
I have here also a letter from the Canadian horticultural council, which quotes the Washington food report issued by the American institute of food distribution in New York city. This is a quotation from what was stated by the American institute of food distribution, in New York city. It is headed "Tariff Gossip", and states:
Exports of dried fruits, fresh and canned fruits and vegetables, packaged cereals and many grocery specialties will be increased by tariff concessions secured from 17 nations with whom we are now bargaining.
Canada will permit us to make larger shipments of fresh fruits and vegetables at lower duties, except during approximately two months of Canadian harvesting. Canada will also open the way to receive larger quantities of canned fruits and vegetables from us which it does not pack itself. It will probably concede lower duties on dried fruits which were kept fairly high under the 1939 agreement because of the empire preference.
Now, with the Geneva agreement, those preferences will be done away with, and we find ourselves in a difficult position. Would labour or industry permit such tactics to be employed to undersell Canadian manufacturers and the products of Canadian labour? They would not submit for one moment to the importation from the United States of large quantities of goods produced here in Canada by Canadian industry. Yet, that is done, so far as the farmer is concerned, and they get away with it.
Bill No. 3 has been referred to as a program, but it is not a program at all. It is an expedient. It is a hoax without faith, and without vision. I say to the committee that you cannot be a great nation on a carload of lettuce. We hear a howl from the cities for these greens. This country was built up on pork and beans, and I am not a poet either. We have the climate and the people to produce these things.
I have mentioned immigration. We could put these immigrants to work. But we must
Foreign Exchange Conservation

have some assurance that once they make some investment, and make plans, they will be able to reap some profit from those plans.
The minister says that this program is non-discriminatory, so far as other nations are concerned1; but it is certainly discriminatory so far as Canadians are concerned. In history we make reference to B.C. and A.D. I expect very shortly we shall be referring to AA.-After Abbott.
If the minister were a fruit and vegetable grower in this country, what would he do right now?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I should like to say a word or two about the Geneva treaties as they apply to vegetable and fruit growers. They are the victims of a squeeze play. Certain fruits and vegetables are allowed in for a certain time; but under the Geneva treaties the length of time United States produce is kept out, because of our production in harvest time, has been narrowed. One vegetable which was prohibited previously for fifty-two weeks is prohibited now for only ten weeks. In other words, the Canadian grower is penalized for forty-two weeks.
In this connection let me refer specifically to a few items. First, cranberries, which were protected fifty-two weeks under the old plan, and with a tariff of not less than li cents are now protected for only twelve weeks with a tariff of three-quarters of a cent. Many other tariffs have been reduced. Green peas which formerly were protected for fourteen weeks with a duty of five cents are protected now for only eight weeks, with the duty reduced to 34 cents. In respect of onions Canadian producers have lost protection for twelve weeks. Rhubarb was formerly protected for fifty-two weeks with a tariff of 1-J cents, whereas now the time has been reduced to ten weeks, and the tariff to one-half cent. Tomatoes were protected for fifty-two weeks; that is now reduced to thirty-two weeks.
Therefore our farmers are the victims of a squeeze play, particularly in southwestern Ontario. We have two huge United States markets in Buffalo and Detroit. When the United States growers see that a surplus is piling up in cities other than the two I have mentioned they will consign the surplus to Detroit and Buffalo. Canadian truckers go over there, buy that distress produce, bring it into the Canadian market and lick the Canadian farmer. That has been going on for years.
The government should take this matter seriously. They are in power because of the

confidence of the people, and I say they are losing the confidence of the Canadian farmer. Farmers have been given no guidance as to what they should do, either in the next year or in the next five years. The month of March is just around the corner, and many of the growers about whom I have been speaking must make their plans in March and early April. I am asking that guidance be given to those producers as soon as possible, so that they may have products to sell-produced by Canadians and for Canadians and to save United1 States dollars.

I should like to deal with something which I am sure the minister will agree is within the terms of the subsection. Although we made a beginning with this the other night, we did not get very far. What I complain about is that the minister of reconstruction seems to consider this from the point of view that it is entirely natural and, no doubt in his mind, a desirable thing that the ordinary life of the community should be invaded. Let me reassure the minister that I am not going to repeat my speech on arbitrary power. Nevertheless I want to reiterate that the business life of the country is being invaded to an extent which six months, or let us say nine months before the minister began to consider this, he probably would have thought was just as intolerable as I hope he does still.
The minister of reconstruction talks about this as if it were the most natural thing in the world. It seems to me that this question of permits must be considered rather particularly. This is a thing which we all deplore. I say "all" because I am sure that all of us do deplore this action w'hich the government has considered necessary and which, under the circumstances, I suppose the rest of us have to admit is necessary to some minor extent. However, I believe that this committee and the people of this country are entitled to know just to what extent it is necessary. speechtext: We are not discussing this or that detail but the basis on which the permits are to be issued. A project approval is not a document which can be used for any other purpose; it is simply an undertaking that the person can proceed with the projects with the assurance that the department will issue the permits necessary to allow him to carry out that project.

I thought that was the picture. There we have the whole complaint of the official opposition on the manner in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce and Reconstruction and so on is carrying on. What is the sense of a scheme like that? If the minister required these powers the government should have come to parliament and asked for them; or, if it could be done under order in council, that is another way in which they could have moved. But here we have a minister of the crown arbitrarily deciding whether or not projects from one end of this country to the other can go ahead. Instead, he writes a letter without any authority whatsoever behind him.
That, Mr. Chairman, is an impossible situation and I am amazed that the government of Canada or of any other democratic country would allow business to be done in that way. We might just as well find out now where we are going, and wThether this is the way in which the country is to be run.
