trade. I have in my hand three documents to which I shall refer by their numbers. These documents are numbered1 10-4110, 1(44120 and 104130. I am not going to read any portions of them to the committee, but I shall summarize as best I can what they mean. They mean this, that to the end of last year our balance of trade from all1 countries, excluding gold, was $237'8 million. The gold was practically $100 million-I believe the exact figure is between $90 million and $100 million. This means that we had close to $350 million, or perhaps nearer to $340 million.
As shown in the documents to which I have referred, for the ten months ending January 1, 1948, our net credits extended abroad were $376 million. On that basis, if you take the twelve months it would be approximately $450 million. Therefore, our credits that we extend exceed the over-all balance which we have. I think what I have said gives us a really /true picture of what our trading position is.
We have been carrying on this program, austerity or otherwise, and it seems to me that what the government have done is to waken from a sound sleep where they have not been watching with their usual caTe the mounting trade balance against us, the dollar position which was constantly getting worse. For three months they have operated under this program. To speak broadly, fthe bill which we have before us does not purport to do more than they are doing at the present time under the authority which is theirs or which they have assumed to be theirs under the order in council passed under the Foreign Exchange Control Act. That act does not expire until sixty days after the meeting of parliament in 1949.
When we remember the draining from the reservoir of goods which took place during the war; when we remember that inventories have been increased exceedingly quickly since the war and certainly very much so within the past eighteen months; when we remember that there has been a heavy stocking up of inventories in view of rumours of the possibility that the action which was taken would never be taken, it brings to my mind the thought that perhaps it would have been better for the government to carry on for another twelve months or for a period prior to the expiry of the act on which they base their present authority, and then the house might not have been bothered' at all with this bill.

The circumstances which I have mentioned, namely, the stocking up by merchants-by merchants, I mean all people selling goods- was such that I believe that within twelve months the situation would have rectified itself to a very large extent or, in any event, would have reduced itself to a trend that was fairly flat. We would have had a much more accurate idea of what our position was in that respect.
It seems to me that what has been done is reminiscent of what was done by Mr. Schaoht, who was in charge of things financial in Germany prior to the war. He had to do two things. He had to develop the economy to run the ordinary needs of the country, and he also had to prepare a great armament program. What he did was this. He simply said, "We will estimate 'the things we need to live and the things we need for the armament program. Therefore we will take control of all foreign exchange arising from German exports and these will be allocated strictly along the lines I have indicated."
Is that not exactly what we are doing here? We are taking charge of all foreign exchange and allocating it through the judgment of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to specific purpose within our own country.
I am not smart enough, I am not sufficiently experienced, nor do I have the knowledge to say that ultimately in Germany, had there not been a war, that action would have failed probably just as quickly as it did because there was a war. What I am trying to say is that the government has been tried and not only has it. been found wanting, but it has led us to disaster and chaos. Do not let any one say that I am predicting that for this country of ours. What I am saying is that it is basically wrong.
It is true that we are told these are only temporary measures. If they be but temporary measures, it seems to me that it should say so somewhere in the bill. The bill is entirely silent with respect to that.
I hope that no one in this country will accept the view which, by inference, may plainly be taken from the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, namely, that exports to Britain in United States dollars are just as good as exports to the United States. I am not saying that it was done deliberately, but that is a complete distortion of fact. The minute they use their limited supply of gold to take care of motorcars, then they have to give up something else. What we would have accomplished is this. It is true that they may

Foreign Exchange Conservation
do the allocating of their limited supplies of gold, but it is equally true that we choke off these people and rid them of all chances to re-establish themselves by trading with us, [DOT]their sister commonwealth.

I want to say something more about this question of permits, and I should like to return to what the minister said on Thursday night last. I should like to read just a sentence or two of what he said. We are talking about the automobile industry, to which the hon. member for Calgary West has referred, and the minister said, as reported on page 1165 of Hansard:
However the point I make is that it seems to us that the industry is capable of contributing much more in American funds than it has been doing, and the regulations are framed with that in mind. I shall be very glad to get the regulations and either put them on Hansard or send them to my hon. friend. I have sent up for them.
I want the minister to tell us about these regulations, and then I want him to give more detailed figures of purchases, imports and exports by the automobile industry. I am not able to find figures which bear out what he said. Even giving the words he used the most favourable interpretation, while I agree fully with the hon. member for Calgary West, it is entirely improper to allocate gold against the motorcar industry and say that is as good as United States dollars and therefore we have a surplus. What I want to know is whether, even on that basis, we have a surplus. The figures I have show the contrary. I should like to hear the minister's figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Since this is not my bill I have not all the figures before me. I sent for them on the day in question and I had them here, but by then nobody seemed- interested, so I put them back in the file. I shall have them here after three o'clock tomorrow afternoon. The figures for the motorcar industry are closely in my mind. I happen to have been examining the position of imports and exports in dollars, and I must say that I was surprised myself to find that, on balance, the exports produced more than was represented than by the drain on dollars through imports.
Does that include tractors?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No; motor vehicles. Tractors are made in Canada only to a very limited extent.
Was the minister talking about automobiles, trucks and parts?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That is right, of a class or kind made in Canada.
Then I am going to suffer a great disappointment tomorrow, because I cannot be here to hear the minister's figures, and I know they are wrong.

Section 3 (2)i(a) refers to goods that have not been delivered- but were in the possession of a common carrier before November 18, 1947, and were in the course of continuous and uninterrupted transportation to Canada on the day preceding that day. That provision is a counterpart of the provision in P.C. 4678. I suggest that that provision ought to be liberalized, if one may use that expression with a small "1" without any political connotations. Many cases of genuine hardship must have been brought to the minister's attention, arising out of the strict enforcement of that provision, and I submit that the provision itself is not a suitable one.
It is axiomatic, as I believe the Minister of Finance will agree, that new legislation ought to avoid any interference with existing contractual obligations unless there is some over-riding principle involved. In the transactions of the kind I shall refer to there is no question of exchange involved. They are cases in which purchases had been made of United States goods before November 17; the money -had been paid, and there was no question of exchange involved. In some of the cases of which I have personal knowledge, the goods had been warehoused or had made perhaps the first leg of a journey, but were not in continuous and uninterrupted transit on the day t-he government chose to put the new program into effect. Those cases were automatically excluded by the act, even though no question of exchange was involved.
Here is Mr. Jones who has the good fortune to have his goods in movement towards Canada, whereas Mr. Smith alongside him had also completed his purchases of United States goods but was waiting perhaps for the proper season or because he did not have storage room or for some other perfectly good business reason, and so his goods were not in continuous and uninterrupted transit at the moment when the new regulations came into effect. I hope that the minister will treat these as cases of hardship.
I do not believe that it will open the door to fraud if you enlarge the exception to include cases of goods purchased and paid for which were not actually in uninterrupted transit on November 18. Surely to goodness,

Foreign Exchange Conservation
ample proof can be 'had that a transaction had been completed, ownership had passed and the purchase price was, paid. I cannot see that there would be any difficulty in policing transactions to that extent.
There is another feature to this provision. Take the case of the Canadian importer who perhaps has stretched his means to the limit to complete a purchase in the United States. He has been wanting to bring the goods in here and has stretched his financial resources to the limit. He has completed his purchase. He is prevented from moving the goods to Canada. He has, therefore, to sell his goods at the best price he can obtain for them over there, to sacrifice them, being at a disadvantage, or in the other case he is up against an equally serious disadvantage in performing his contractual obligations. I wish the minister would give the committee a clear assurance that, in cases where purchases had been completed and there can be no question whatever of any other requirement of United States dollars being involved, the mere fact that the goods were not in continuous and uninterrupted transit at one minute after midnight on November 18, will not prevent importers from bringing in goods which are theirs in fact, and where there is no question of United States dollars being involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That question was given most careful consideration before the provision was put ini the order and a test of continuous and uninterrupted- transit was accepted1 as the one which should be followed. The particular hardship clause is there to be availed of in cases where the importer would suffer exceptional hardship by reason of the fact that he could not bring the goods into Canada because they were not in transit at the time the order came into effect. In the case of the importer who had paid for the goods in the United States, he, of course, became the -owner and he could warehouse them there if he wanted to, or he could sell them and bring the proceeds back into Canada and that would represent a conservation of United States dollars. Th-e provision was 'based' on the experience of other countries in imposing similar restrictions. Sweden had to take similar action last March, and where they attempted to recognize existing contracts the restrictions did not become effective until six months after being put into force. There has to be a line drawn- somewhere, and there is the hardship clause to take care of exceptional cases. As I said to -the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, a considerable number of permits have been issued under the -hardship clause, some 5,000 odd, representing goods of a value in the order of $7,000,000.

In section 3(1) the minister is given power to "issue, vary or revoke permits for the import of such goods '. I have looked carefully through the act many times to find1 a provision- which clearly defines the conditions under which the minister may revoke a permit, once granted. It seems to me, with respect, that once a permit has been granted, it should no-t be revoked except under clear circumstances, for instance, where there has been fraudulent misrepresentation to the minister in support of the application. There ought to be clear provisions in the bill some place, not necessarily here, dealing with the matter, and it should not be left simply to regulations to define the circumstances under which the minister may revoke a permit which he has issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was discussed to some extent this afternoon, and I pointed out that it is the language which is used in the Export-Import Act. The question of revocation of permits relates more particularly to the quotas which are, as the committee appreciates, a form of permit. For instance, if a quota holder should go bankrupt, his permit, consisting of a quota, should be revoked. If he fails to distribute the goods equitably in the district in which he is doing business; for instance, if he has a quota of import oranges and does not distribute them equitably we should have 'the -power to revoke his permit. Suppose an importer in- Halifax, for example, has a large quota of import oranges, and distributes them all in the Halifax area, and does not send any over into Sydney-I am just using that as an- illustration-it is desired to have the power to revoke his permit if he does not distribute his quota fairly. I think under a permit system, unfortunate as it may be, it is necessary to have the power to revoke accompany the power to issue. I agree with my hon. friend that it would probably be as well, in drafting regulations, to try to indicate as explicitly as possible the conditions under which permits would 'be issued, varied or revoked; but in the very nature of things it would probably be impracticable to foresee all the circumstances under which it might be necessary to exercise that power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This subject of revocation is an -important one. I agree with my hon. friend that it would be desirable to try to spell out just as completely as possible in the regulations what these conditions are, but hon. members will recall that during the war it was necessary to have control measures of this kind. Unfortunate as it may be under ordinary circumstances, it is necessary to their effective administration in the interests of the public that there should be a considerable measure of legislation by regulation.
Bureaucratic control.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One may describe it as he likes. I am afraid it is inevitable, and one cannot make these control measures work without them. I do not like them any better than anyone else. I had hoped we would be out of these things long before this; nevertheless sometimes it is necessary to do unpleasant things. This legislation is an unpleasant necessity, and if it is to work, and work smoothly and properly, there must be the flexibility that is necessary to enable it to be done. One of the methods is by the enactment of regulations which are made public, which have to be published in the Canada Gazette, and which the public know. But to attempt to spell it all out in a statute, to foresee all the various circumstances which will arise in a statute, I suggest is completely unrealistic. It would defeat the very purpose which we are trying to accomplish.

I have not taken any part in this discussion and I do not intend to take much no-w. I had occasion this afternoon to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealing in his usual cavalier way with questions asked by the opposition. I can
quite understand the attitude of the minister, because he had been flitting from power to power, until today he believes that, as far as parliament is concerned, it is just an institution before which he appears from time to time. But when asked questions he uses the usual method he has of referring to the statements made by those in the opposition-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Thank you very much.
Well, I am glad to receive at least thanks from the right hon. gentleman. That is quite different from the usual-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Was it something you wanted to know after all that?

All I -have to say, sir, is this. My right hon. friend invariably resorts to abuse when asked questions that are reasonable and fair. I can quite understand his attitude. He has passed through one dictatorship to the other. He took over radio; he controlled air, and now he controls wheat marketing in- this country; and finally he is going to control the entire economic development of our country. I point out this in connection with what the hon. member for Eglin-t-on said, when we place in the hands of a minister the absolute power that has been placed in the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, surely parliament has a right to ask that these powers shall be exercised in- accordance with law and statute passed by parliament or regulation which parliament knows of. I ask the minister this question: is that an unrealistic suggestion?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend gets himself mixed up with parliament as a whole.

As a matter of fact, sir, when I see the powers that are conferred here I look back and I read what the Prime Minister said in 1933, and I ask myself, has democracy so changed in this country? In the session of 1932-33 the question of the allocation of power to the executive was under discussion, and the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 3187 of Hansard'.
If this parliament parts with the power of parliamentary control over legislation generally and- places that power in the hands of the executive, I say, we shall find very soon the contention being made in different parts of the country that if one individual or executive can exercise all -the powers of government then a class can just as well do the same.
Sir, I suggest this to you, never in the history of this country, and even today in Britain under socialism, has any minister been as

powerful as the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this government today. It is not very long ago in the city of Toronto that he made a great speech after coming back from Britain. He pointed out the great danger of placing almost absolute power in the hands of one man. He spoke of its danger and how such a condition of affairs would not be permitted to exist in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: When was this?
That was in a speech made in Toronto in October last.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: To whom?
To the board of trade of the city of Toronto, after the minister's return from abroad.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I never addressed the board of trade in the city of Toronto in my life.
It just indicates how the minister forgets some of the statements he makes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I never addressed the board of trade in the city of Toronto in my life.

I suggest to the committee that if we are to make the progress which the committee desires we should stay within the rules of the house and discuss the clauses which are before the committee.

That is what I am
trying to do, and I wish to thank you, sir, for having pointed out that there is reason for the minister's change of attitude, because I was referring to statements made before he became Minister of Trade and Commerce. Does Your Honour say to me that, in connection with the question of powers, I may not refer to some of the lessons of democracy given this house on occasion?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it would be more strictly in accordance with the rules, now that we are in committee, that members should discuss only the clauses before us, and not discuss other questions which, though relevant to this question, are not strictly before the committee at the present time.
As long as you keep me directed so that I shall stay within the rules, I will try to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: When do we come to fundamental rights and freedoms?
Every time we deal with you we come to them.

Fundamental rights and freedoms. That expression coming from my right hon. friend is just a series of words, not practised by him at any time.
Now, for the purpose of building up what I have to say, may I finish the quotation? Incidentally, may I say to my right hon. friend that I said that it was the board of trade, and that this was the only institution he spoke to in Toronto after he came back from abroad. I believe it was the businessmen of Toronto.
The Liberal businessmen.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Again, I cannot see what that has to do with the clause under consideration. I believe the committee does want to proceed with its work and I again ask the hon. member to discuss clause 3.

I have sat here and listened to the debates that have gone on and have not had anything to say, and I heard a discussion this afternoon, and even this evening, which I considered relevant to the section in question, as were the remarks that I was making. However, Your Honour rules this committee and I bow to your ruling.
I was dealing generally with the question of controls, and I am sure Your Honour will not consider me astray if I refer to a statement made by the Minister of Finance a few moments ago in regard to bureaucratic controls.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was my hon. friend's phrase, not mine.
Yes, but accepted with approval by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not necessarily with
approval.

He certainly does not disagree. You know, sir, we have come to this point in this country. All along, those on this side have spoken about bureaucratic controls and how the people have been strangled and stifled by them, and now the minister admits the necessity of bureaucratic controls this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Controls, anyway.

He admitted the necessity of bureaucratic controls. As a matter

Foreign Exchange Conservation
of fact, that is a long cry from the Prime Minister's statements of a few years ago. I am sure he will admit what the advisory council of the national Liberal federation enunciated at the recent convention. Here for the first time is an admission by those who direct that party that bureaucratic controls are, in fact, necessary in Canada. I read from the section dealing with fiscal policy:
The advisory council of the national Liberal federation reaffirm its faith in the system of free enterprise, accepting the proposition that government of bureaucratic control or regulation may become necessary in an economy based upon a system of free enterprise.
It gives various reasons why bureaucratic control is necessary, and finally declares:
... to overcome a crisis developed by a temporary emergency.
That, sir, is the greatest admission we have ever been able to secure that there is, in fact, in this country, and has been, bureaucratic control, and it is part and parcel of the policy of this government.
May I ask this question-? When did the Minister of Finance first seek an opinion regarding the use of the Foreign Exchange Control Act for a purpose which parliament never intended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My recollection is, early in August.

Early in August. At that time the amount of our foreign exchange was gradually going down. It had diminished to a great extent at that time. The situation was dangerous. I will not give quotations on this occasion; but not only did the hon. member for York West warn the government in June last, but throughout the summer newspapers in the country were warning them. Yet, did the government act? In August, the minister admits, he realized the situation, because if he had not realized it he would not 'have gone to the law officers of the crown to find out if there was not some way whereby he could get around that situation. I say, with all the respect I have for the Minister of Finance, that no more serious insult to parliament has been committed by any minister than by the Minister of Finance when he admits that parliament was led by the government to believe that this act would be used for one purpose only, and the government, in the face of the promise to parliament, endeavoured to ascertain whether they could circumvent an act passed by parliament for one purpose in order to achieve another purpose.
That indicates how far this government was prepared to go in order to circumvent parliament. If the situation was serious in August, why then did the government wait until November 17? Why was parliament called? Why was parliament not called during that period? Why was it necessary to do something that has never been done before in history, to impose taxation by order in council? Why, if this government intended to respect parliament, was not something done between August and November 17 to convene parliament? That is the question to which I think the minister will have to give a better answer than the rather offhand, haphazard answer that he has given up to the present time.
I am now going to ask the minister certain questions, and they can be answered either at once or later as the case may be. How much United States currency is it estimated that during the period of a year will be saved on prohibition; that is, on commodities directly prohibited? And on commodities subject to quota-on automobiles, and on tourist expenditures in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have given some of that.
You have not given all of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I can give some of them. As I have said before, we estimated tourist expenditures at $30,000,000 to $40,000,000; but that can only be an estimate. I think I can probably give the prohibitions and quotas right now if my hon. friend will wait for just a moment.
Very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is estimated, between prohibitions and quotas, at approximately $300 million. I do not know that I have a breakdown of the articles on the prohibited list and those on the quota list. That is based on last year's importation of those articles.
That is a full year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be operating for a full twelve months' period; that is correct. I can perhaps give that in a little more detail tomorrow or a little later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
It is impossible to make an estimate. We can make estimates in various

Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I obtained my
information from the London Free Press of November 19, and the estimate on new gold given on that day, as reported, was $50,000,000. I should also like to ask the Minister of

Trade and Commerce what have been the savings to date in those various items. I do not know which minister to ask. Possibly I will ask the Minister of Finance. What have been the total savings to date under those various items?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is impossible to say, because we have had only' a couple of months of operation. Any estimate of the savings must be made on the assumption that the volume of imports, on both prohibited goods and imported goods, would continue at the same rate as they had during the preceding twelve months. The best criterion or a partial one is the position of our exhange account which I gave the other day. At the end of January it was approximately $514 million, up from a low of $461 million, I think, on December 17. But it is hard to pinpoint the savings in this group or that group. We shall have monthly figures under tariff item classifications for the prohibited items and for the quota items.
The minister has none of those yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We may possibly have the December figures. I shall have to check on that. We would not have anything later than the December figures, but we may possibly have a breakdown on those. I would have to check on that and see.
If the minister has those, he will let us have them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

On the occasion of this conference the Minister of Trade and Commerce allegedly stated that certain industries in this country were to be given priority because they are capable of expanding exports to the United States; in other words, in the granting of permits for the importation of capital goods, certain particular industries were to be given priority. Has any determination been made as to which these industries are? Are there any regulations which indicate that a definite policy in that regard is being followed?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I have stated several times that in the issuing of project approvals, approvals are given for industries which are improving the United States exchange situation. A good many have been granted. I suppose my hon. friend will ask to whom they have been granted. I cannot give him that information just now, but it is a routine procedure. A considerable staff is engaged in exactly that work of determining whether the project is one that will improve Canada's

United States exchange position. If so, the approval is granted. If, on the other hand, it is a project that will be a drain on the United States exchange position, the project approval is not granted.
But are there no regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Definitely.
Are no definite principles enunciated?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Definitely.
That is what I am trying to get at.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.

Will the minister lay on the table of the house a copy and let us see the general principles on which he acts? I am sure he will agree that that should be the case. If that is not so, the situation lends itself to discrimination on the part of the minister. In other words, it places the minister in a position where he can say to one manufacturer in a certain industry that he will give him no permit and to another manufacturer of a like product that a permit will be granted. Unless there is something of a definite rule, the minister might very well find, however he might back up and be adverse to this being considered, that political fitness would become the qualification for the issuing of permits. It is in that respect that I ask the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend is taking that from the sewer of his own mind.
What is that?
You are doing that from the sewer of your own mind.
Mr. Chairman, that is a typically polite remark on the part of the minister, and I ask for an immediate withdrawal of that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: In the last eight years I have had probably more opportunity than any other man in public life to favour my political friends and punish my political enemies, but never on any occasion have I had an insinuation that it is a thing that I am likely to do; and I will not take it from my hon. friend or anybody else.
I am accepting the minister as being the custodian of all perfection. Nevertheless, I want that statement withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I will not withdraw it.
I suggest that the hon. member for Lake Centre withdraw his insinuation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Probably the language on both sides has been quite strong. The Minister of Trade and Commerce used the word "sewer" which, I think, is probably too strong. Perhaps he would like to change that word.

Withdraw.

I am pointing out, as the hon. member for Vancouver East stated, that without regulation executive tyranny is possible in a case such as this. The minister has now stated 'that under no circumstances should such a thing be said. Then I ask him what possible objection he could 'have to accepting a regulation so that each industry would know whether it qualifies to receive a permit for the importation of capital goods from the United States. In that way every suggestion that unfairness is possible, that caprice has been exercised, that injustice has been done by way of discrimination will be removed entirely; for each and every one who applies will realize that in certain industries permits will be granted, if extensions will meet the exchange situation, whereas in other industries permits will not be granted, regardless of circumstances.
After all, the identity of the individual minister of the crown is not at issue here. The matter at issue is that parliament is asked under this legislation voluntarily to give up and to surrender its rights and to place them in the hands of one or two ministers to determine for an indefinite period.
It started off with the minister's statement that in a few months everything would be well. But since this debate has started, that "few months" has become an indefinite date in the future. We ini this parliament are asked to give power which might not be of an emergency nature, and which may be permanent; for all the record of the last few
[The Chairman.]
years has shown that when parliament has surrendered! a power temporarily, in the ordinary course of events that power has tended to become permanent, and a complete loss on the part of parliament, and its right.
Will the minister not reconsider the situation?-I make an appeal-and if I cannot make it to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, then I make it to the Minister of Finance-to reconsider this, and to tell the committee in some businesslike detail, so that he who runs may read and understand, what general principles are to be adopted. So far as permits are concerned, in respect of capital goods, those industries which will not receive permits should be designated, and those which will receive them should also be placed on the list, showing that applications from them would in ordinary circumstances be affirmatively accepted.
On the occasion of the press conference- and I have various press reports here-the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated, as it is reported in the Ottawa Journal of November 18, that the government would encourage and increase the production of coal. And he indicated that, in order to increase the production of coal in Canada, the government might be more generous in the matter of subsidies. Then he went on to say that it would even consider assistance in the export of Canadian coal, if paid in United States dollars. I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce what, if anything, has been done to carry out the suggestion or plan enunciated on that occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I did not hear the reference. The hon. member referred to the Ottawa Journal.
It was a statement made at a press conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Every pound of coal that has been produced in Canada has been marketed, and every encouragement that I know of, has been given. If a subsidy was required to move boats, or to move coal1 by ship, such subventions have been provided. If boats have been required, assistance has been given to obtain boats.
Have there been any subventions since November 18?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
Extra ones?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Nothing outside the scope of the subventions, but there have been new applications.

Probably the minister could tell us which companies received extra subventions since November 18?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Dosco.
And who else?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That is all.
That is all?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Those were the only subventions required.
Were there any other applications?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.
No other applications?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: What clause is my hon. friend speaking to now, Mr. Chairman?
That is what I want to know.

I am speaking to the question of a permit. After all, we are granting certain powers to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but we in parliament do not seem to be able to get a complete answer to these questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not believe the question of subventions is involved in this, although the question of permits is.
Surely that is part and parcel of the general situation we are discussing.

speechtext:
Coal1 subventions, do you
mean?
Yes.

speechtext: What section in the bill?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 3 carry?

The minister has just taken exception to a remark made. I wonder if he could explain the necessity for what seems to me otherwise a quite unnecessary and indefinite state of suspension in connection with Canadian industries. He spoke earlier this evening of a list of what he called project approvals. As I understand the proposition, the Minister of Finance is in a position to give a permit to anyone who applies for imports. Why should the minister of reconstruction take it to himself; why should he have the power, or why should he follow the course of writing a letter saying, "Your pro-5849- 814
ject is one in connection with which I might give a permit," or "I will give a permit when the permits come into force." Why could the Minister of Finance not simply get the approval or advice of the minister of reconstruction and give the permit now? Why put the thing on the. precarious basis of a letter which says, "At some time in the future I may give a permit"?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: A project might require a vast variety of permits. It might require a permit for the importation of structural steel, a permit for specific items of machinery and so on. It is all very well to give permits, but the applicant is not ready to specify his requirements, and there is no purpose in asking him to file under every tariff item that may be involved since the assurance can be given that if and when he needs permits he will obtain them.

I rise to a question of privilege. This morning no less a person than the Prime Minister extended greetings to the leader of the C.C.F. party. The hon. member for Renfrew North extended greetings to the hon. member for Selkirk. I want to extend greetings to the hon. member for Greenwood who has returned for his annual visit. I hope he is fully recovered in health.
That was totally uncalled for, if I may say so.
Do I understand the minister to say that he then gives tentative approval for applications which may be received in the future? Is that the effect of the letter of approval?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: A manufacturer may want to erect an industrial plant, and he desires to know that if he undertakes a project of that kind he will be able to procure the United States contents required by the project. He asks that simple question and he obtains from the Department of Trade and Commerce either a yes or no answer to his question. If the answer is yes, he is able to proceed with the project knowing that he will obtain his United States contents. If the answer is no, he does not start his project and get himself involved because he has received pretty fair assurance that he will not be able to build it.
Is this letter a tentative application?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Call it that if you will.

I am. just trying to find out what reliance the manufacturer or the person who is considering a project can place on that letter if he has not made application.

Foreign Exchange Conservation
I am trying to find out upon what basis the minister says that he will or will not give permits when application is made.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The application is made on a form and the facts are examined by the appropriate officers. If the project is of any considerable size the applicant appears before t'he officers of the department and gives them any explanations they require. Then the facts are presented to me with a recommendation and a letter is issued accordingly, or approval is issued accordingly in the form of a letter. My hon. friend wants to know if it is binding. The man does not have to go through with his project because he gets approval and therefore it would not be binding on him-. If a minister of the crown writes a letter, it is binding on the minister.

I understood the minister to say earlier in answer to the hon. member for Lake Centre that at least one reason for his being hesitant about making regulations along the line which were suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre and which seem to me to be absolutely sound was that it was still too soon to determine just how much currency could be allowed to this or that industry. If the minister is not sure, when project A comes in, that he will allocate so much to the steel industry or so much to the motorcar industry or so much to some other industry, how is he able to decide on the project? How is the man who is undertaking the project to know whether this is decided on some general principle, or whether it is just the absolutely uncontrolled decision of the minister, based upon no reason that anyone can hold the minister to?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Perhaps he will not be able to decide that, but at least he will know whether he can go ahead.
I imagine it is really a waste of time.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I think so.

But maybe it is 'time we have to waste. The minister is supremely uninterested, absolutely uninterested in the idea of people having rights. The minister laughs. I think the idea of rights is something that he considers rather ridiculous. Apparently his colleagues have given him this power. We have objected in this house to order in council government, but we have got away beyond that. We shall soon be looking back to the days of order in council government and thinking that that was a

good time, that we had the judgment of at least a dozen men, some of them good men; but now we have only the judgment of one minister, even though he has a lot of portfolios.
We have not yet been able to interest the minister in our idea. I know very well the minister regards this house as being a tiresome place. He is bored when he has to come here >to talk to us. He regards it as a waste of time and he shows that by his demeanour, I will not say never, but he seldom tries really to answer our questions in a way w7hich will satisfy us, as some of his colleagues do. His whole attitude is that it is rather impertinent to ask questions. That is the impression I get. But I am going to ask this question and I am going to keep on asking it until the minister answers it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I understand that my hon. friend thinks it is the inherent right of any man to build anything he likes, provided that he has the money to pay for it.
That is just a rhetorical answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: You asked me a rhetorical question.

No, I did not. I recognize that we have got into strange times, partly due to the action of the government, if you like, but I will not emphasize that; I recognize that we have reached a point where we have to use some unusual expedients. All we are asking is that we have some remnant of the liberties under which we used to live. I think there are some ministers here who would like to leave us with some residue of those liberties, but, so far as the minister of reconstruction et cetera is concerned, I do not think he is interested in the idea.
I think we should stay here until we either get him interested or get somebody else interested. The hon. member for Lake Centre asked a reasonable and sensible question. He asked if there were any regulations, if there was anything anyone could appeal to. I put *that up to the minister. He asked me if I thought any man in Canada could build anything he liked just of his own sweet will. That is not a serious contribution to the situation. All I am asking is whether there is something short of the minister's uncontrolled jurisdiction, whether there are some means whereby a man will have some rights other than those granted by the minister's sweet will.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Now we are getting on common ground. I more than any man in this house believe that people should have the

Foreign Exchange Conservation
widest possible freedom to spend their money [DOT] as they like, and I have explained to the committee the difficulty of administering building control on that very ground. The present regulation has reference to only one view point. Is the project helpful either in earning more United States dollars or in saving United States dollars? That is the test. If it is a factory, what does the factory make? Is it something that can be exported? Is it likely to save dollars by avoiding an import? Is it likely to be convertible into an export? If it cannot meet two of these tests there is every reason why the project should not proceed. If it simply adds to the amenities of living the permit is not issued. If it simply adds somewhat to the comfort of the situation it is not likely to be issued. We have a larger capital expenditure program planned than this country can afford. It must be cut back. Its cut back is dependent on the value of the project in the present economic situation.

I think that is a sensible explanation and we are getting on common ground at last. But I cannot believe that is the exclusive test, because the minister himself the other day said a thing that, I imagine, is correct. He said that, so far as individual items are concerned, if it is a replacement of a worn-out part, the permit would issue automatically. That is in contravention of what the minister has just said, because it would apply to any company whether producing United States dollars or not. There must be other regulations as well. That does not come within the four corners of what the minister said a moment ago.
Coming back to what the member for Lake Centre asked, we have asked repeatedly that the regulation shall be published so that people will have some knowledge of what their rights are. I do not think that is an unreasonable request. The minister is going to bring down tomorrow the regulations for the motorcar industry. That may give us a pattern which can be applied elsewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I think I explained earlier that we are drawing up regulations for industries as rapidly as we can; but, naturally, before publishing the regulations, we have to test them carefully. It might be all very well for some of our officers to sit in an ivory tower and plan regulations for a great industry having ramifications all across the country. Those regulations might look good here in Ottawa; but, until they are tested against the industry as a whole and the repercussions of
their application are estimated, it would be dangerous to file them. It might do a great deal of unnecessary harm.

The minister said that the project will be approved according to whether it earns or saves United States dollars. For what period of time does the minister suggest that this test should be applied? Must it earn or save United States dollars within a matter of six months or a year, or is it five or ten years ahead, or something of that kind? Can the minister say what is in his mind now as to the period of time that will govern his judgment in making a decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It must be obvious to my hon. friend that the time must be flexible. The last project I saw that came up for approval was a pulp mill on Vancouver island. It will not earn United States dollars for eighteen months, and yet it will contribute to the permanent solution of the problem we are tackling. I hope my hon. friend will not quote me now as saying that it must be eighteen months. If it is six weeks, so much the better.

We had made a little progress. We find that a project which might earn United States dollars in eighteen months will get a permit. Is the minister thinking further ahead, of long-term additions to capital expenditures on development of the country, whether or not they would save United States dollars? During this period of restrictions, will capital development be permitted only if it saves United States dollars, or might there not be circumstances under which an industry suitable to Canada, but which does not replace United States products, would be permitted to be constructed?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If my hon. friend will mention one industry I shall try to give him an answer.

Has this program not resulted in a shortage of United States refrigerators and boxcars coming into Canada which might have been used for the shipment of Canadian goods back to the United States, thereby securing United States dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Does my hon. friend want cars to ship potatoes?

There used to be 1,000 cars a day come in from the United States loaded with fresh fruits and vegetables and other produce. Immediately this order went, into effect, these cars stopped coming into Canada, which cut off our supply of cars for the shipment of Canadian goods back to the United States, thereby preventing the ship-
Foreign Exchange Conservation

ment of Canadian goods across the line which would have brought in United States dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I would be very sorry to know there were shipments of Canadian goods which were not crossing the border because we had not the cars. I thought we had an ample number of cars for our shipments to the United States.

I may inform the minister that there is a great shortage of cars, especially refrigerator cars which come up from the United States loaded with fresh fruits and vegetables. We used to ship back in those cars potatoes from Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and probably Ontario, which brought in United States dollars. The same is true of boxcars. As soon as this order went into effect, the Canadian railways refused to allow their cars to go across to the United States, because they did not want them to come back empty. Only coal cars are coming in now from the United States, and they are not suitable for shipping Canadian goods such as newsprint, potatoes, pulpwood and many other goods which would have brought in United States dollars. As soon as this order went into effect, it created a great shortage of cars.

To refer to my earlier question, what about machinery for a sawmill or logging machinery imported from the United States for use in the lumber industry? These would not necessarily come in under permit for definite projects. It cannot be decided that the importation, of any one of these articles is certain to produce more United States dollars. There must be a closer definition than the one he gave to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario; there must be a closer definition than the simple criteria. How is he to know whether the approval he gives earns more United States dollars than the money spent for the equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: To my simple mind, if a lumber dealer wishes to bring in more machinery I would assume that that machinery would have the effect of increasing the exports of lumber from Canada, and thus be an earner of dollars; therefore I would give the permit. My hon. friend might have doubts, but I think that would be a reasonably clear case.

But surely a great deal of the lumber cut by such machinery would be consumed in Canada; a great deal more would go to the United Kingdom, and a great deal more to Australia, and the amount of lumber which that mill might send over to the United States might be negligible as compared with 
its total cut. Is that not a correct statement? The minister will know that as well as I.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It might be reasonable to my hon. friend, but, as I say, the simple souls who administer this would say that lumber was for export, and therefore the importer of lumber machinery would come within the class of goods for which permits are issued.

Do I understand from that, for instance, that an unlimited number of lumber carriers would be allowed in? If the mill showed the minister that it needed these carriers in the ordinary course of its business, would permits issue automatically for these things, or is there some other restriction the minister has in mind that he might apply in the event that too many people applied for the importation of such goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If the machinery was required it would be demonstrated that logging machinery was required, and if it was not available from a Canadian source the permit would issue. I will go that far dogmatically. I hope the hon. member will not cross-examine me too much on it.

After an experience of sitting in this House of Commons one does not expect to find consistency in the government; one does not expect to find consistency in their statements. For instance, in almost every debate in recent times in this house in which the government has taken a position of some kind or other, it has been possible to turn up speeches made by the present Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition, in which precisely the opposite position was taken by him. In what we have heard tonight from the Minister of Trade and Commerce and others, we have just about a complete contradiction of the things that the same right hon. gentleman has previously said.
You recall, Mr. Chairman, April 1, 1946, in this house. You recall that the same right hon. gentleman made a statement of some importance at that time concerning building control in Canada. I am going to read you the statement in a moment, but, before I do so let me remind you what the minister has just said by way of justifying the pyramiding of a system of control throughout the length and breadth of Canada over these capital projects, pyramiding to an apex on top of which the Minister of Trade and Commerce is himself squarely perched.
This is one paragraph from the; speech made by the right hon. gentleman on April 1, 1946. It will be. found at page 411 of Hansard of 1946. He, said:
During the war years, the Department of Munitions and Supply maintained a rigid con-

Foreign Exchange Conservation
trol of construction for the purpose of providing material for the war. During that period our citizens accepted this control as necessary for the successful prosecution of the war and its regulations were observed. However, after the end of the war, construction control regulations were no longer observed to the same degree.
Mark these words if you will, Mr. Chairman:
It was recognized by the department that it was impossible to judge from Ottawa the essentiality of different projects and the local conditions which necessarily must govern each decision.
Just let me remind you of these words, Mr. Chairman:
It was recognized by the department that it was impossible to judge from Ottawa the essentiality of different projects . . .
The whole basis of the case put forward by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in asking parliament to vest him with these powers that might have made Mussolini swoon with envy is that he may be completely trusted to exercise these powers not only without favouritism but also with complete perspicacity, complete ability to judge what is essential and what is non-essential. One need do nothing more than to offer to the right hon. gentleman his own words that it is impossible to judge from Ottawa the essentiality of different projects.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no simple test then as there is today, though.
No simple test then as there is today?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right. The simple test today is whether it will get us United States dollars.

The Minister of Finance has not been following what I am saying. The minister's statement was not made during the war. This is the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, then the minister only of reconstruction and supply, on April 1, 1946, with reference to the situation which followed the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know.

In the first sentence he talked about the war. Then he goes on to say, now with the war over, it is impossible to judge from Ottawa the essentiality of building projects, and for that reason he abandons the construction controls which were the means he had in his power at that time for channeling into the construction of houses available supplies of building materials. He turned his back on that responsibility and said, the whole reason is this, we cannot tell from Ottawa what is essential and what is not; therefore we will withdraw from the field.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We can tell from Ottawa whether a project will save United States dollars or not.
I bet you cannot.

What is the difference in essence between a national emergency arising out of a shortage of houses and a national emergency arising out of a shortage of United States dollars? The principle at stake here is precisely the same. If it was impossible in April, 1946, for the minister to judge the essentiality of building projects at Ottawa, just how much easier is it for him in February, 1948, to judge the essentiality of capital projects in the matter now before us.
All this talk we have had tonight about trustfully leaving to the minister and his judgment to decide what is good for the country and what is not simply does not hold water. The fact of the matter is that we are back to the same old situation from which we thought that democratic peoples had emerged1 several centuries ago, where justice was measured by the length of the chancellor's foot. In this case, apparently, the essentiality of measures of this kind, capital projects, is simply to be measured by the particular notion that the Minister of Trade and Commerce entertains at the time the particular application comes before him.
In what I am about to say I am not necessarily being unkind to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Human nature being what it is, there is not a man, I do not care who he is, the. minister of reconstruction or anybody else, who is so constituted, that, given powers of the scope and breadth of these powers which he is seeking in this bill, can dismiss from his mind all vestige of whim, caprice and favouritism when applications come before him. What is bad in this measure can be cured only if the minister is stripped of those dictatorial powers, and if what is necessary to meet an emergent situation is dealt with in terms of statutory provisions that cannot be applied otherwise than equally to all people, regardless of who they are.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the clause carry?
May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether he is to have any control over projects which do not require United States material?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.

It is clear that there is control only over projects which will require at least some United1 States material.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: How would the other projects come to me? Why would they come to me?

Well, things, both good and bad, seem to have a way of coming to the minister. I was just wondering. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance a question. Last week there was some discussion with regard to the possibility of the government taking some steps to promote the purchase of goods in Canada, or from soft currency countries, to replace purchases from the United States. At that time the minister was not clear as to what steps the government was taking. Can he explain to the committee tonight what is being done along that line?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The principal encouragement is, of course, the way in which 'the quota system is working. There is a decided incentive to Canadian importers to search for commodities and merchandise in soft currency markets, because the size of the quota is such that they can bring these in readily. There is no effective limitation of certain lines for the time being. Textiles is perhaps the outstanding example in that field, fresh fruits being another; and, as far os automobiles are concerned, I believe there is a fairly generous quota. I am told there have been continuous discussions with representatives of the United1 Kingdom, Australia and other soft currency areas to see what additional imports can be made available to Canada, and the trend is upwards, as the figures I gave this afternoon indicate. I am confident that this will be tremendously accelerated over the next two or three months, and we are particularly anxious that it should take place in textiles, which used to be a traditional export from the United Kingdom to Canada. For the past two or three years we have had to replace them with expensive textile imports from the United States. There is an indication that what I have indicated will be achieved.

AVhat about an effort being made to have Canadian goods purchased to take the place of goods prohibited from the United States? I have two of the minister's advertisements, and in neither is there any forthright suggestion that Canadians should endeavour to purchase Canadian goods. No emphasis is put on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have been urging that. Perhaps it would be desirable to advertise along those lines. The purpose of the advertisements to which my hon. friend refers was that they should be more in the nature of directives, that they should be informative.

I approved the copy myself. I wanted it to be non-controversial and not to be considered as propaganda for the particular policy, but wre found from the letters that there was a considerable amount of misunderstanding as to where people should go for information, and just what the program covered. Therefore those two advertisements were put in the papers across the country, the intention being to clear up some of these misunderstandings. I have not decided whether to spend more money on that sort of thing. That decision has not been taken.
The minister will agree that there is little indication of a change in the future whereby Great Britain will be able to supply us with United States dollars as she did before the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But she can supply us with goods, which is just as effective.

There is not much indication that in the near future there will be a drastic change in the present general position; and if we maintain these prohibitions against goods for a certain period and then lift the prohibitions, we shall be right back in the spot in which we now find ourselves. I suggest that some steps should be taken to reach a permanent solution of the problem, and one way would be to persuade the Canadian people to buy their own Canadian goods or goods from soft currency countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We hope they will do that.

There is one other question I should like to ask the two ministers. In one of these advertisements there is a picture of an oil drum, a coal scuttle, a bale of cotton and a steel rail, and it says: "To keep our industries humming, our living standard high, we need petroleum, coal, cotton, steel and similar essential things." I take it that these are the four products which are primarily responsible for our shortage of United States dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those are the four products which we import in substantial quantities. Steel products of all kinds ran to something like $500 million last year. I am speaking from memory. Cotton runs to a large figure, and petroleum is something like $250 million or $260 million. These are tremendous items; they are all essential, and they have to be paid for in cash.
Those are the four commodities which we purchase in the largest quantities from the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that is correct, yes.

What plan has the government in mind to produce petroleum, coal and steel in Canada? I realize that we cannot produce cotton, but what plan has the government in mind to produce the other three items? I know, and I presume every other member in the house knows, that we have the potentialities for producing large quantities of each of these commodities, and this is the time there should be an all-out drive to produce them. I should like to know, therefore, what the government has in mind in regard to some such plan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No doubt the Minister of Trade and Commerce could answer that better than I can. So far as petroleum is concerned, that depends on discovery. There were fortunately some important discoveries of petroleum in the Leduc field south of Edmonton about a year ago. Active exploration is being carried on by a great many who are interested, large companies and others, to see where further supplies of petroleum are located in Canada. Steel production is being expanded. As my hon. friend knows, the steel company at Hamilton is expanding its strip mill and Algoma is expanding. That takes some time.
What about iron production?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I have not much personal knowledge of that. We have all read, of course, of the explorations going on near the Labrador border, but some little time will elapse before the material will be available for active use in the steel industry. It would appear, however, to be quite an important discovery. All these things are going on. They will not solve the short-term problem, however, though they are of importance, as the hon. member has pointed out, in the permanent fundamental solution of the question.
What about coal?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are getting beyond the scope of the bill, which deals with restrictive measures and not constructive measures. I do not think the discussion we are having at the present time is relevant to clause 3.

I am reading from the government's own advertisement with regard to the austerity program; we have to get at production of those commodities before we can get out of our present difficulty. I submit that both the minister and I are in order in discussing these commodities.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In my opinion, both hon. gentlemen are out of order at the 5849-82
moment. The hon. member for Vancouver South is dealing with another program, a constructive program, and the minister has replied. I think the committee must deal with the bill which is before us at the present time, the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act, which deals with restrictive measures entirely.

Would not the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South relate to exchange; for instance, coal of which we import a large tonnage? We have to pay for that in United States currency. Does that not come under the problem of exchange?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member could deal with permits respecting the importation of United States coal.
At the moment in Toronto, on Yonge street, in the store of A. Welch and Son there is a demonstration being shown to the public in the burning of Alberta coal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not .think that is in order at the moment. The hon. member will have plenty of opportunity to discuss that question.

I wish to make one or two observations and to ask some questions. When we impose controls we seldom know where -there will be repercussions, and I think it should be brought forcibly to the attention, not only of the committee but.of -the people generally, that we find as a result of these controls, as my colleague, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton pointed out a shortage of freight cars coming into the maritime provinces from the United States to take back certain vegetables grown there. The Canadian railways do not want to send their cars loaded with Canadian produce to the United States, because they do not know what, if -anything, will come back in that type of car; and the Americans are just not sending up as much by way of railway freight as formerly. So there is a shortage of cars, something -that -the government could hardly have been expected to think of.
The hon. member for Vancouver South asked the minister of reconstruction if permits were required only for imported materials which would be used in construction. That is clearly the case. May I just ask for some opinion from either one of -the ministers on the effect on the price of certain construction projects in this country. If I may call them that, when you have certain domestic supply, let us say of steel for construction or of machinery, and the excess requirements which we do not pro-

duce in our own country we import from the United States. In order to save the trouble of going to the minister and getting a permit, you naturally try to get your requirements in the domestic market, and surely the temptation is to bid up for quick delivery and avoid the uncertainty, and difficulty of going to the minister. Therefore I should think another reaction we shall have from these controls, particularly in the capital goods industry and under schedule III of this bill, is that we shall find an increase in price, because it is more convenient, if you have the money, to pay rpore and avoid going to the ministers for a permit.
I have a question of a more general nature which I should like to direct to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Will he expand on those general principles which guide him in giving an O.K. or refusal to applications? He said as he has said before in this house, that the principle was whether or not an application would save United States exchange or produce United States exchange. I tried to call to mind the things which would be the subject matter of applications and, in view of the fact that our economy is so closely integrated with the United States economy, I wondered just what we would import or what would be the subject for the application for exchange that would not either create United States exchange because we would export something made by the machinery we got in, or would not save us United States exchange? What is there in our own economy here that we cannot, by way of substitution, get from the United States, or what do we make in our own country that we cannot send to the United States? I wonder just how this rule is to be applied as a sound rule, and it is the substance of this whole measure. It seems to me to be broad in its application. I confess that I have had of course, no experience with applications. The minister may have had sufficient, though, to give the committee a little more information.
I think the general opinion throughout the committee is that we are putting a tremendous amount of power in the hands of one or two men, a power which we do not like to see in their hands, particularly in peacetime when we should be able to get along and still preserve all our fundamental rights. So I would ask him to elaborate on that matter.
I should also like to ask how much exchange we are expecting to save altogether. As I recall it, it was $300 million under consumers goods and $200 million under producers goods, or abou t $500 million in all. That figure was certainly given press publicity; whether or not it had

any authenticated source, I do not know. We know that we are running behind on United States exchange by about $1,000 million a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We were.

We were. It may be that they are stopping the flood which was due to the fact that we over-indulged ourselves during the summer months and in the fall; however, time alone will tell. But $500 million is not as much as we should like to -save if we are to balance the account and perhaps restore the surplus of $1,500 million 'that we had a year ago of United States exchange in gold. So, in the absence of rules under this bill, and no business knowing whether or not it is to be put out of commission in order to save more exchange, I feel that the government should give all the information possible and try to give some indication of whether or not we are to be faced with further austerity. The Minister of Finance may well say that it depends on just how the exchange balance is during the next few months. I think it would be interesting for the businessmen to know whether or not they are in a business-and I am thinking particularly of the importing business-which might be blitzed, because further austerity measures are necessary in order to bring about some financial balance.
Just to close my remarks, I should like to make a suggestion to one minister, and perhaps to both of them, particularly with regard to schedule III: It is that whenever a decision is made, it should be published; that a body of laws or a body of rules-call them administrative rules if you like-should be published, so that the Canadian businessmen who have to make these applications will know how other cases have been dealt with, will know if their case is on all fours or on three legs only with a case which has been decided, and will be able to tell approximately what to expect. It will also be a useful guide, if I may say so, to the minister himself, because he will have his previous decisions before him; he will have the reasons for having decided thus and so; it should simplify his judgments for him, just as for a court of law which relies on precedents in order to make its judgments. If this power is taken by the government-an unprecedented power of great magnitude,, and one which we all are sorry to see them take, even if it is necessary-I hope that they will publish their decisions and give a brief statement of the facts. As the Minister of Finance will recall, at the head of the report of a legal case there is a brief review of the facts, a few paragraphs, and then the decision.
