I suggest that the same procedure be followed here so that there will be some guide, some check and some precedent for the public to follow, by which their actions may be guided.

On this matter of permits and controls I should like to ask one question which has been put up to me by several manufacturers in this country. It is this. Will Canadian-owned goods now being processed in the United States require a permit to bring them back to manufacturers in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that some manufacturers can get an export permit to export steel, have it processed in the United States and bring it back into Canada again through the customs. Although it may be on the prohibited list, they will get an export permit to have it sent to the United States to be processed, and brought back in here in a finished state.

I might cite just one item that is owned by the government, namely, 11,000 or 12,000 fur seal skins. They are now being processed in the United States. I cannot find in any of the schedules where a permit has to be issued to bring those back to be manufactured in Canada. The Canadian manufacturers are anxious to find out whether they can bring those back in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall take note of my hon. friend's remarks. I believe it is under consideration at the present time.

I should like to ask a question with reference to the bringing in of machinery. I have had information from certain firms respecting job sawmill machinery required for the keeping of sawmill saws in order. Up to the present time they have been unable to get permits, owing to their not being ready. Is there some reason why the permits are not ready? If so, when will they be ready for the admission of such machinery? It is quite an inconvenience to these people.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: When do they want to bring in saws? They can bring in all the saws they like at the present time.
Not saws; machinery for the sharpening of saws.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: They can bring that in too at the present time.
Are permits being issued for the importation of green vegetables from the United States?

None for lettuce?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Cabbage is good enough.

By the terms of the bill before us I am convinced-and I believe this must be in the minds of hon. members generally- that this is a great step toward departing from democratic government. I have listened to the questions asked and the answers given, and I am just about as confused now as are those who have been giving the answers. No one knows exactly what we are heading for, although it has been suggested that we are heading for a dictatorship. We have the whole framework right here, sufficient completely to wreck our own democratic system.
This just did not happen overnight. We have had, during the course of this debate, sufficient evidence to prove where the government made its fatal error. On July 5, 1946, the then minister of finance placed an artificial value on the Canadian dollar. That was the date when the natural flow of goods between nations was prevented.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
What I am saying has a direct bearing on the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As the hon. member says, it has a direct bearing on the bill, but not on the principle of the bill.

We are discussing import
controls.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The principle of the bill has already been accepted. We are now dealing with section 3, and the discussion must be related directly to that section. I would ask the hon. member not to proceed with a discussion of the principle of the bill.

If we are to confine ourselves to section 3, then I still say that we are delegating to the minister extraordinary powers which he will have great difficulty in administering fairly. I think that can be said, in fairness to the minister himself.
How are people to plan any project, when they have to come to Ottawa to find out what the score is. There exists a terrific state of confusion, which all results from the fact that the government is interfering with the natural process of regulating trade and commerce. One simple method of avoiding all this was already in existence.
What yardstick is the minister to use when he must determine whether or not a permit is to be granted, when he must determine that a permit is to be revoked, or that a person who is in possession of a permit cannot dispose of his business and his permit as well? He has no equity in the permit, according to the terms of the bill. So what method can any businessman employ to determine how best he can carry on and make a contribution oi

United States dollars-and that would appear to be the purpose of the bill? That man has no security in the bill, except at the pleasure of the minister-one man. What method does the minister propose to employ to determine what course shall be pursued?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is so easy for a businessman to put his problem before the department and to obtain a ruling, that I suggest it would be much easier to do that than for me to answer a theoretical or hypothetical question on the floor of the house. I do not know just how to answer the hon. member's question.

I should like to ask a question arising out of a statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He said that so far as building or construction projects were concerned, those responsible for building the projects would be told to use Queenston limestone instead of Indiana limestone. If the minister is going to say to construction companies that they must use Queenston limestone instead of that from Indiana, the Queenston quarries might not be in a position to supply the required amount of limestone. It might take years to reach a position where it could be supplied in quantity.
I asked the Minister of Finance a question a few days ago, but 'he did not answer it. I ask it again. Are these suppliers to be given no security? If they expand so as to build up a big business in an effort to supply limestone for these projects, they might find that these restrictions would be taken off overnight, and a company which has spent huge sums of money to expand might be swamped. Can not the government say to the producers and to the manufacturers of Canada how long these restrictions may last. It is important that this question should be answered. It is a question 1 am sure private members who are supporting the government as well as the members of the opposition would like to have answered if they have factories and producers of goods in their own constituencies.
I am wondering if the government are not finding themselves in this position, that the government having agreed to the terms of the Geneva trade agreement for freer trade, this bill setting out restrictions is just the opposite; the two courses of action are counter to each other? In the terms of the Geneva conference we have agreed to freer trade; yet the government is now in a position where it is putting on restrictions. For that reason the government will not say to the people of Canada, "This will be in force for six months" -or two years or ten years, as the case may be. I think it is important to every member

of parliament and to the people of Canada as a whole to know how long this program will be in effect, in order that they may make provision to take care of short supply. If they do build up a business they should1 know that they will not be wiped- out again by the lifting of restrictions. Surely the question I have asked is a reasonable one.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
It illustrates the difficulty of answering a hypothetical question. I used Queenston limestone as compared with Indiana limestone as an example. The saving of United- States dollars would not be great, because neither Indiana nor Queenston limestone is used in such large quantities. So, for that reason, the hon. member has -me in a somewhat awkward situation.
However, I would say this, that I think any business which expands to take care of the immediate situation, thinking that it will last more than a year or two, is making an unwise investment. I hope it will not do that. Unless an industry is expanding on a basis that will survive under normal conditions, it would be unwise to expand.

The Minister of Finance says that this is not a protectionist policy, that it is an emergency policy. I agree in principle that the government is adopting a program which should have been adopted in this country twenty years ago. I know the government will not adopt a conservation policy because the Conservatives have advocated such a policy. I believe that if a policy of this kind had been inaugurated twenty years ago we would have built up industries in this country, thereby creating employment and preventing the exodus of our people to the United States. If we had in Canada a conservation program we could process our own natural resources, instead of just ti-ying to preserve United States currency spent for imports, and we would be doing something constructive for Canada.

Hon. members have been waiting patiently for some announcement from the government, because in previous times when the people in other parts of the country have spoken the government has made announcements with respect to by-elections. I wonder if the spokesman for the government would give us the results in Huron?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: They cut down the majority greatly.

How many extra customs officers will have to be appointed under this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the figures at the moment. Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue could give that information later on.

Getting back to the point raised by the hon. member for Durham with regard to industry, I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce a particular question having to do with importers. I have had an inquiry from a company which is in position to build up a business in Canada in mirrors. They have spent some money on capital goods, and then to their surprise they find that their place in the schedule has been changed and that mirrors are being imported from the United States. They are afraid that their capital expenditures will be a loss. The first definite guidance we have had was when the minister spoke a moment ago and said that he hoped new industries would not be built up as a result of these restrictions and embargoes. Could the minister elaborate on that statement and let the committee know whether it applies to all categories of industry and whether it is his policy not to build up Canadian industry behind tariff barriers?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I have read in the papers about doing it with mirrors, but I do not understand what my hon. friend is doing with mirrors. The principle is simply this. If an industry wishes to establish itself in Canada; if it is one which in normal times would be able to operate profitably; if it is an industry which will assist in building up exports or in conserving United States dollars, it will be welcomed. But if it is an industry being built up simply to take advantage of the temporary prohibitions, it will not be welcomed. For instance, if someone wants to come in here and build refrigerators in Canada for no other reason than that the importation of refrigerators is temporarily banned, that industry will not be welcomed. If we recognize it for what it is, it will not be permitted.

The minister says "come in." This is the case of a Canadian company wanting to expand into new lines. They admit frankly that they cannot compete with large producers in the United States who can export to Canada over the tariff barriers.

I just want to follow up the argument advanced by the minister in connection with the development of industry. He is warning against it. A great deal of coping, window frames, door frames and that sort of thing has been imported from Ohio and Indiana. Many buildings are finished with that type of finish. The Queenston limestone plant has been in existence for a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am sorry I mentioned it.

You have mentioned austerity and there are a lot of things you are going to be sorry over before we are through. Queenston limestone is a marvellous stone, but it is about four times as difficult to mill as other limestone because it is so much harder.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I advise you not to buy it.

You have to have coping and trim of all kinds, even in new structures. I wanted *to take up this matter privately with the minister. Some new construction was being considered and the first thing asked about was the use of Indiana limestone. I told them that it looked as though they would have to use Queenston stone, which would cost them more money. What is the position of the Queenston quarries so far as going ahead and stimulating production' is concerned? In the face of what the minister said tonight, they will be right back in a short time to where they were before. The inconsistency of his statement is apparent on its face. I cannot see where the minister's argument holds at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is nice of you to do the worrying for the Queenston quarry.
It is not just the Queenston quarry I am worrying about; it is that the principle behind this thing is all wrong and I just want to point that out to the minister.

There is one matter that has been discussed recently in this house with some fervor on the other side, namely, beneficial results of publicity being shed on transactions of a certain kind. I wish we could discern in the remarks of the ministers the same zeal for publicity with respect to government business and policy under this act as they have shown in connection with publicity in the affairs of others.
What assurance have we under this bill that favouritism will not be exercised in its administration? The Minister of Trade and Commerce says that we can trust him, but that is not a good enough answer. There is nothing in this bill that says there shall be a statement given to the public as to what permits are granted, what permits aTe denied and what things are permitted to be brought in by way of permit.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I should
think, Mr. Chairman, thait the question is out of order because it does not pertain to section 3.

We are dealing with permits under section 3, and there is the clearest provision there that:
No person shall import or attempt to import into Canada any goods listed or of -the classes described in schedules I, II or III except in accordance with a permit issued by the minister.
I do not like the system set up by the -bill, and section 3 is the core of the bill. I would think the minister should be very glad to improve his measure somewhat by at least giving us assurance in statutory form that star chamber methods will not be practised in the administration of this -measure. What is there in the bill that gives any assurance to the public that everybody is to be treaited alike, that all -persons who come or send to Ottawa for permits will receive equal treatment of their application- on their merits? There is nothing in the bill -which says the minister shall give any publicity to whatever he does under it. When it comes to reports to parliament-and this is what the Postmaster General had in mind-section 9 provides:
The minister shall lay before parliament, within- fifteen days after the commencement of each session thereof, a report on -the administration of this act during the preceding fiscal year.
That means that the minister can go ahead for the whole of 1948 without having to make a report to anybody-not until fifteen days after the commencement of the 1949 session. In the meantime, permits could have been granted to one -and denied to another in equal circumstances and the public would know nothing about it. That situation is not one that can be tolerated by any democratic parliament in the twentieth century. Methods of that kind we thought were discarded three hundred years ago. Where do we get any -assurance in this bill that it is not just a case of star chamber methods that are to be practised with respect to applications under the bill? It is time we had some assurance from the government, not that the affairs of individuals shall be disclosed to the public, but that there will be published regularly, at short intervals, statements with respect to the commodities imported under permit, so that the public can have some idea of what is going on under the bill when it is passed, and have the assurance that the full benefit of publicity is being cast upon the administration of the measure with respect to the issuing of permits and that it is not being used to cover up favouritism.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have already answered that question several times. After most careful consideration, it was felt that in the case of capital goods the only system which could

be made to work was a permit system, and that involves the exercise of discretion. Under the quota system, that is done automatically. The government may determine from time to time what the base period may be and the percentage of imports during the base period, but that applies right across the board. As to capital goods under schedule III, reflection will show that by its very nature, this does not lend itself to any general rule which would be applicable in all cases. It has been indicated' that in certain categories there will be regulations-the automobile industry is one

and so far as possible that will be done. But there are bound to be a great many cases in which there will have to be an exercise of discretion. Suppose some newspaper decides that it must have a large new printing press. You cannot lay down a general rule for that. Permission will be given or refused upon the merits. If some other way could be found no one would be more relieved than- the members of the government, but our dollar situation is such that we cannot continue to allow the uncontrolled import of capital goods into this country from the United States.
If there is any justification for the permit system, then surely, there must be the need for publicity and no reason why full publicity should not be given to the granting of permits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot see any objection to publicity. I do not know just what my hon. friend has in mind-monthly reports or something of that kind. I think it might be possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We were looking into the question of permits and under one item alone, 427-a, the basket machinery item, we estimated that some 15,000 permits would be issued. If my hon. friend wants all those published I will arrange for it if he will pay for the cost of publication.

The minister is treating the committee with his customary levity and derision. I do not suggest that every permit should be published, or that the private affairs of individuals should be disclosed, but there should be disclosure of the capital goods that -are permitted to enter. It should not require too much ingenuity or labour on the part of government officials to make reports on what capital goods are being admitted. That would give people who are interested in that type of goods an opportunity to know whether they were being treated the same as the next man. I was very glad to hear the Minister of Finance say that he would take the suggestion of publicity into consideration, because I think it

Foreign Exchange Conservation
is highly desirable that the public and the house should be reassured by some measure of that kind such as regular reports.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think any reports that could be published would demonstrate that everyone was receiving exactly the same treatment. You could give figures as to the categories of goods brought in and the permits issued, but the man who was refused a permit might still wonder why he was not getting the same treatment as the other fellow.

Should he not have something by way of information to go on? For instance, if he sees that other people are getting permits for importations under the basket machinery item while he is refused a permit, he will ask why permits are being granted to others and not to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It all depends on what they are using the machinery for.
The minister mentioned 15,000 permits under the basket machinery item. Can he give the committee any idea as to how many permits will be issued altogether for all the items?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I gave one estimate because I happened to know that item.
If it is 15,000 for one item, it is probably half a million for the lot.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Not that many.
Mr. SKEY-: How many would the minister say?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It might be 25,000.
And 15,000 under one item alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not know and neither does my hon. friend, 'so why pursue this further? I was just giving a general idea.

It is strange that the minister could make an estimate in regard to one item but has no idea how many permits will be requird in another item. I think the committee is entitled to a little more information. If he has to hire a staff of two or three thousand people to pass on these items it may require months to get an item through. If that happens, the whole business will be held up while his small staff struggle to cope with the flood of requests for permits. I think the minister should give the committee some idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Twenty-five thousand permits a month would be a fair idea.

This matter of reports of what the minister does is of the utmost
importance to the country. As I have said before, the minister is arrogating to himself tremendous power, the power of life and death over a great deal of Canadian industry. It is an important matter, and if it costs a bit ol money to publish the information about the decisions I do not think the committee will have any objection to it. Surely the Minister of Finance, who is familiar with reports, understands what it is that I am after and what a good many other hon. members have in mind. All legal cases are not reported. The 15,000 county court cases or the 25,000 division court cases are not reported. Nobody is interested in them because the principles are well laid down. But on cases which make law, important cases, someone makes a digest of them consisting of three or four paragraphs; it may be a couple of pages if it is very difficult, and that information is given to the public. If a summary were made of the decisions it would give the people who are applying for these import licences some idea of just what the government has in mind when it is applying this one simple principle, does it earn or does it save United States exchange? The principle is so simple that the minister said, in reply to my colleague, the hon. member for Eglinton, it could readily be administered from Ottawa; whereas the deciding of whether or not a particular piece of building construction in some other part of Canada could not be decided from Ottawa.
This is a relatively simple matter. The object is very simple. There will be a few hard oases, undoubtedly, until we get a body of principles. If it is to be such an important matter to Canadian business, we must know what the law on this principle is. It will not go to rest in the mind of the minister and have my support in this house, and I do not think it will have the support of many others on this side of the house, if the minister is to have the matter in his own control and discretion and we are not even permitted to know after the event, much less before.

I do not think we have got very far this evening in finding out how this principle is to be administered. Even at the cost of repetition, we might well pursue it farther. As I understand the situation, at the present time we have a very simple principle, whether it earns or saves United States dollars. If one may judge from some of the answers the minister has given, the principle is so simple it is like a sieve; anything will go through it and it is not a safe principle to work on at all. The minister himself will not be able to pass judgment in his own mind just on that one principle; otherwise it would be

impossible for him to do more than guess whether a thing would earn or save United States dollars. In practice, he will have to formulate a series of sub-principles or subclassifications under which goods will be allowed in.
I want to ask him this question. Is it to be: first come, first served? Suppose, for instance, the minister were to make up his mind that the over-all quota for capital goods was $750 million in a year. The first lot of applications comes along, and he approves up to $750 .million on the basis that these goods are going to earn or save United States dollars. Then someone else comes along with another project which, in the minister's opinion, will earn or save more United States dollars than one of the schemes he has already approved. Will he then cancel one of the earlier ones to which he has given approval and thereby enable this greater saving to be made, or will he stick to what he has already done and force Canada to do without the project which would have saved more dollars than what he has already approved? Can the minister comment on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend asked a long question based on a hypothetical theory, the theory being that we are going to say we shall spend $600 million and no more. We are not going to do that; therefore the whole question falls to the ground.

I am, of course, not satisfied with that answer at all, and I shall wait here until I get an answer to the question. I shall ask my question in two parts, so that the minister can understand1 it. The minister was not listening before-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I listened' to it.

The first question I shall ask is this. Is it a question of first come, first served, and those who come after the over-all quota has been used up are out of luck, regardless of how useful their scheme is?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That question falls to the ground because, as I have explained before, there is no over-all quota. If we can get a great many products that will produce substantial quotas of United States exchange we shall be glad to take them.
Then the whole thing is a grand guess.
In that case why have the schedule at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Why have this debate at all? I cannot imagine why my hon. friend rose in his place.

We are in this position now. The minister has said that any capital goods project will be permitted. That is the sum and substance of what he said, because the test he applied in an earlier question I asked! was ridiculous. In the case of many capital goods, he cannot tell whether they will be used to manufacture goods which will go into the United States or will take the place of goods we would otherwise import. They may all go to soft currency countries. There is no way in which he can tell that; therefore if his answer is that he has no overall limit, and, so far as I can see, the whole thing falls to the ground completely. Is the minister not really in this position, that any capital goods which will increase the production of goods in Canada he will approve. Is that nob the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.
Will the minister give an example? He has been asking us for examples. He must have some knowledge of these things. Will he give us an example of the capital goods which he will not approve?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If a man wanted to build a factory to make billiard tables, for instance, I would say no, we do not want that business.
Then the minister is putting it on the basis of luxury goods, apparently.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: You asked' me to name one and I named one.
I am speaking of a classification. The minister will not allow a Canadian to manufacture luxury goods-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Why not class billiard tables as sporting goods ah well as luxury goods? My hon. friend is really putting on a very silly performance. I enjoy it, but it has taken a good deal of time.

I shall have to take my chance on whether it is a silly performance or not. We may get somewhere this way. Has the minister made any attempt or have his officials made any attempt to classify these capital goods as a guide to the exercise of his discretion?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.

He has made no attempt, then. I think that answer is a pretty good exhibition of what we are getting in this bill. The Minister of Finance said earlier it would be very difficult and almost impossible to make this classification.

Foreign Exchange Conservation

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a matter of appreciation of the facts in individual cases. Surely that is self-evident.

It is quite apparent from what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has just said that the government has made no attempt to bring out a list of regulations which would be a guide to themselves and to Canadian businessmen as to what goods should or should not be imported. It is one thing to say that it is impossible; it is another thing to say they have not made an attempt to do so. I submit that before this committee approves a section of this kind, giving these arbitrary powers whiijh we have talked of so much, at least the government, if they still pretend to have any respect for parliamentary institutions, should attempt to produce a statute which is in line with previous parliamentary practice. If they had come in and said that they had tried and failed and that this was a great emergency condition, we might be more disposed towards this scheme. But when they come and say they have not even tried, then I think an attempt should be made before we approve the section. I wonder if the minister will answer this question. Has he made any attempt, since he cannot codify those things he will let in, to codify those things he will not let in?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That is the opposite of the other.
Would it not be a shorter list, the ones he will not let in?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not know.

You do not know. The great mind has not been exercised. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a man who has been resourceful in everything for the past seven or eight years. I should think that if he would exert himself and set the great mind in motion he might produce something which would satisfy the members of the committee. I do not like this situation where no attempt is made to bring into the house a bill which would accord with proper parliamentary practice.

I think this is an unedifying and, in a way, a rather humiliating proceeding. I do not think we are an unreasonable lot of people over here. We have been asking for information and, as far as the minister of reconstruction is concerned, with the exception of one brief interlude when he has tried to help us, he has been in the highest degree unco-operative.
I think section 3 should stand over because, in any event, the minister of reconstruction
has to bring in information which he should have had here tonight. He says he will bring it in tomorrow. Second, I hope the Minister of Finance will consider the point brought up with regard to the word "revoke". If he will not consider the point, we shall have something more to say about it.
In the third1 place, I want to add to the point made by the hon. member for Vancou-ve.rJBurrard. We are not suggesting that there must not be discretion. We recognize that there must be. But what is being done is, in effect, appointing a committee with no terms of reference. We are asked to vote for this absolutely blindly, without any restriction, although I would point out that the bill itself does not contemplate that. In section 5 it is provided that the governor in council may make regulations governing the issue of permits for the import of goods listed in schedule III. I presume the order in council will not be merely a statement that the minister of reconstruction shall issue what permits he likes. I should hope it would not be that, and it is highly reasonable that we should ask now, before voting for this section, remembering always that this is an extraordinary invasion of our rights, that some attempt should be made, as apparently it has not yet been made, to lay down at least certain principles. As a matter of fact, some of the things the minister says tonight make one feel that there has been no attempt at all. I do not think that is quite true, because on the other hand he has told us that there have been regulations, though we do not know what they are like, in the automobile industry. If there have been, I see no reason why there cannot be framed certain general' regulations, the principle of which would be effective in other cases.
I am suggesting, therefore, that this section be stood over. If the minister will not accept my suggestion I shall regret it. If he says it cannot be done tomorrow, I see no reason why the bill should not stand over another day. We are well within our rights in asking that an attempt be made to have at least the terms of reference or something equivalent to that. I therefore suggest that section 3 be stood over for the reasons I have given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no desire to rush the section through if anyone wants to discuss it, but I may as well say now that I do not think it will be possible to give to the committee the full regulations which will have to be prepared and drawn up under the enabling powers contained in section 5.
Foreign Exchange Conservation

I do not want the minister to make me look unreasonable and1 dogmatic. The minister speaks of the full regulations which will be needed in order to make it operative. I do not think I said that. I said, some general principle. I used the words, "terms of reference", something in the nature of a guide of some kind', which up to the present time we have not had. At present we are asked to sign a blank cheque.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a fairly good guide in schedules I and II. Schedule I is a straight prohibition and schedule II is the quota. It is true that the regulations will establish the base period'. It is now done under the existing order in council, and it will establish the percentage of imports during that base period. That is automatic. That is the principle, so that the discussion this evening is related almost entirely to the individual permits, if I may so describe them, under schedule III.
I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Literally they will be
legion. You may have groups like the automobile industry, where regulations can be drawn up, laying down a principle. But so far as the rest of the schedule is concerned, it must be essentially a matter of the exercise of discretion by the minister. I am fully aware of the objectionable features of that, and the discretion must be exercised in this way, that it involves the appreciation of facts in- a great many individual cases. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce will agree with me that in categories where one can lay down general principles, such as the automobile industry, which is a good example, regulations can be adopted and made public so that everyone can know them. But I am certain that, after all that is done, when one has examined a number of industries where that can be done, there will be a large residuum of cases where you simply cannot lay down a general principle, and there will have to be an exercise of discretion. I am almost sure that will be the case.
We gave a tremendous amount of thought to this matter when the legislation was contemplated and, as I believe I said before, we reluctantly came to the conclusion that the only way in which schedule II could be made to work would1 be under the permit system. That, I know is a general explanation.

The minister has conceded, I think, a good deal of what I said. I do not disagree with his

statement that there will be many that cannot be brought within a definite rule. On the other hand, he has agreed that there may be a great many that can. What I complain about is that, so far as I can see, except in the case of the automobile industry, no attempt at all has been made to do it. I see no reason why we should be asked to vote on this section until that attempt has been made. If it was even the case that the minister was coming in and saying, "Look, we tried to draft these things and found we could not do it", that would be something. But we are not even in that position. We are told that in the automobile industry that has been done. We are to see that. A moment ago the minister suggested, if I understood him correctly, that in other large and important areas it might be done. We are asking to have that done; that is to say, we are asking to have whatever can be given in the way of a general yardstick or of general rules. We do not intend to be unreasonable and say that you have to dot your i's and cross your t's; but, as I said a moment ago, at the present time we are being asked to sign a blank cheque. There has been no attempt to do what we are asking. I must say frankly that what has been done so far has not been wholly reassuring because, according to the figures I have, the minister's statement with regard to the automobile industry is wrong. Tomorrow it may turn out that my figures are wrong, but I do not think so. Therefore it is not reassuring to go ahead and sign this blank cheque at the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On this particular section, I do not know that one can give much more information than has already been given. It enunciates the general principle that imports require a permit when they come from certain areas. There is no trouble with regard to schedules I and II.
I do not think there is any trouble there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I said before, one must freely admit that under schedule III there must be a wide measure of discretion. The situation at the present time is that no permits in fact are being required for the capital goods group, and they will not be required until March 1. That delay is in order to work out a good deal of this detail which I think my hon. friend is perhaps referring to-to look into such cases as that of the automobile industry and some of these others and see what the regulations will have to be for the exercise of the discretion which must be exercised in

Foreign Exchange Conservation
connection with these schedule III cases. But at the moment individual permits are not required.

I am coming back to my point. The minister has not yet said anything which makes me feel that even he thinks my request is unreasonable. My request is for what general rules there are that can be laid down. There are some. Perhaps when we get the regulations in the motorcar industry the thing may look a little bit clearer.
I wish to ask one other question here. The minister says that no permits are required until March 1. Is it not correct that, while that is no doubt strictly true, in fact have not people been warned that they must watch their step with regard to any undertaking they are contemplating now just as if the regulations were in effect? In other words, are the regulations not, to all intents and purposes, in effect in respect of any work which people are taking up now which requires imports from the United States? Will the minister say if that is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It has been announced publicly, over the radio and in varieus statements in this house, that if anyone is contemplating a project which requires imports over a considerable period of time, particularly after March 1 next, he would be wise to have his project approved and to make sure in advance that he will be permitted to import from across the line the materials which he requires.
Which minister has charge of issuing the permits under schedule I? Is it the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have.

The agility of my younger friends enables them to rise to their feet more rapidly 'than I am able to do, but I had intended to ask a simple question. What happens when goods arrive here which are in schedule I and are not permitted to enter? I have a simple example. It is in connection with a small shipment of goods ordered from Scotland last summer. Two days after the issue of these orders or prohibitions, they sailed from Scotland, passed through the Panama canal and have now arrived at Victoria. They are being held at the customs at Victoria. They are urgently required by the firm which ordered them. They are of no use to anybody else, because the firm's name is stamped on the packages. Are they to be thrown into the sea?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. On the facts as my hon. friend has presented them, a permit would be given under section 4 of this measure and the corresponding section of the order in council. It is a case which would be treated as one of hardship. The goods would be useless in the other country and they would be allowed to come in.
How would the firm go about getting them in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Write a letter to the emergency import control division, Sussex street.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the section carry?
Carried.

No, it is not carried. I said to the minister that I thought this section should stand, because we still have to get certain information in regard to the regulations with respect to the automobile industry. I am confident that the Minister of Finance will take some action along the line I suggested with regard to regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know what action can be taken. Of course the section will have to stand. It can be talked on until eleven o'clock. I was hoping that we might make some progress. There are other sections of the bill under which I think any information could be given which could conceivably be wanted. But I am in the hands of the committee. I thought that in six hours we might get one section through.
Section 3 stands.
Progress reported.
